Calculus · Part III · Integrals

Module 11Techniques of integration

Integrate products, powers of trigonometric functions, square roots of quadratics and rational functions, by parts, with identities, with trigonometric substitutions and with partial fractions. You will also learn to choose a method, to check a computer’s answer, to recognise integrands with no elementary antiderivative, and to bound the error of a numerical approximation when the integrand has the required derivatives.

⏱ 270 minYou need: Modules 1 to 10, especially the product and chain rules (Module 5), the derivatives of Modules 5 and 6, and antiderivatives and substitution (Module 10)

In this module you will

  • Integrate by parts, choosing uuu and dv,dv\mathclose{\text{,}}dv, repeatedly or in a table, in definite integrals and to derive reduction formulas
  • Integrate powers of sines, cosines, tangents and secants with identities and substitutions
  • Evaluate integrals containing a2−x2,\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}\mathclose{\text{,}}a2−x2​, a2+x2\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}a2+x2​ or x2−a2\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}x2−a2​ by trigonometric substitution, and return to xxx with a triangle
  • Integrate rational functions by long division and partial fractions
  • Choose a method, check a computer’s answer by differentiating it, and recognise integrands with no elementary antiderivative
  • Approximate integrals with the midpoint, trapezoidal and Simpson’s rules, and bound their errors
1

Integration by parts

Module 10 turned the chain rule round and got the substitution rule. This section turns the product rule round. Products are everywhere in integrals, xcos⁡x,x\cos x\mathclose{\text{,}}xcosx, xe−x,xe^{-x}\mathclose{\text{,}}xe−x, x2ln⁡x,x^2\ln x\mathclose{\text{,}}x2lnx, exsin⁡x,e^x\sin x\mathclose{\text{,}}exsinx, and Module 10 warned that there is no product rule for antiderivatives: an antiderivative of xcos⁡xx\cos xxcosx is not 12x2sin⁡x\tfrac12x^2\sin x21​x2sinx (Section 10.1).

Start from the product rule of Module 5, (fg)′=f′g+fg′.(fg)' = f'g + fg'\mathclose{\text{.}}(fg)′=f′g+fg′. Read backwards, it says that fgfgfg is an antiderivative of f′g+fg′.f'g + fg'\mathclose{\text{.}}f′g+fg′. So if you can integrate one of the two terms, you can integrate the other. Try it on xcos⁡x,x\cos x\mathclose{\text{,}}xcosx, with f(x)=xf(x) = xf(x)=x and g(x)=sin⁡x,g(x) = \sin x\mathclose{\text{,}}g(x)=sinx, so that fg′=xcos⁡xfg' = x\cos xfg′=xcosx is the integrand and f′g=sin⁡xf'g = \sin xf′g=sinx is easy:

ddx(xsin⁡x)=sin⁡x+xcos⁡x.\frac{d}{dx}(x\sin x) = \sin x + x\cos x.dxd​(xsinx)=sinx+xcosx.

So xcos⁡x=(xsin⁡x)′−sin⁡x,x\cos x = (x\sin x)' - \sin x\mathclose{\text{,}}xcosx=(xsinx)′−sinx, and an antiderivative of the right side is xsin⁡x−(−cos⁡x):x\sin x - (-\cos x)\mathclose{\text{:}}xsinx−(−cosx):

∫xcos⁡x dx=xsin⁡x+cos⁡x+C.\int x\cos x\,dx = x\sin x + \cos x + C.∫xcosxdx=xsinx+cosx+C.

Check: ddx(xsin⁡x+cos⁡x)=sin⁡x+xcos⁡x−sin⁡x=xcos⁡x.\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\sin x + \cos x) = \sin x + x\cos x - \sin x = x\cos x\mathclose{\text{.}}dxd​(xsinx+cosx)=sinx+xcosx−sinx=xcosx.

Theorem 11.1Integration by parts

Let fff and ggg have continuous derivatives on an interval I.I\mathclose{\text{.}}I. Then, on I,I\mathclose{\text{,}}I,

∫f(x) g′(x) dx=f(x) g(x)−∫f′(x) g(x) dx.\begin{aligned} &\int f(x)\,g'(x)\,dx \\ &\quad= f(x)\,g(x) - \int f'(x)\,g(x)\,dx. \end{aligned}​∫f(x)g′(x)dx=f(x)g(x)−∫f′(x)g(x)dx.​

That is: if GGG is an antiderivative of f′gf'gf′g on I,I\mathclose{\text{,}}I, then fg−Gfg - Gfg−G is an antiderivative of fg′.fg'\mathclose{\text{.}}fg′.

Proof

The function f′gf'gf′g is continuous on I,I\mathclose{\text{,}}I, so it has an antiderivative GGG there, by Part 1 of the Fundamental Theorem (Section 10.4). By the product rule,

(fg−G)′=f′g+fg′−f′g=fg′(fg - G)' = f'g + fg' - f'g = fg'(fg−G)′=f′g+fg′−f′g=fg′

on I.I\mathclose{\text{.}}I. So fg−Gfg - Gfg−G is an antiderivative of fg′.fg'\mathclose{\text{.}}fg′.

∎

In Leibniz’s notation, put u=f(x)u = f(x)u=f(x) and v=g(x),v = g(x)\mathclose{\text{,}}v=g(x), so that du=f′(x) dxdu = f'(x)\,dxdu=f′(x)dx and dv=g′(x) dxdv = g'(x)\,dxdv=g′(x)dx are their differentials. The formula becomes

∫u dv=uv−∫v du,\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du,∫udv=uv−∫vdu,

read “the integral of u d v is u v minus the integral of v d u”. To use it, split the integrand into two factors: u,u\mathclose{\text{,}}u, which you will differentiate, and dv,dv\mathclose{\text{,}}dv, which includes dxdxdx and which you must be able to integrate. The formula trades ∫u dv\int u\,dv∫udv for ∫v du,\int v\,du\mathclose{\text{,}}∫vdu, and it helps when the new integral is simpler than the old.

Example 11.1Three integrals by parts✓ Checked

Find (a) ∫xe−x dx,\displaystyle\int xe^{-x}\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}∫xe−xdx, (b) ∫ln⁡x dx,\displaystyle\int \ln x\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}∫lnxdx, for x>0,x > 0\mathclose{\text{,}}x>0, and (c) ∫arctan⁡x dx.\displaystyle\int \arctan x\,dx\mathclose{\text{.}}∫arctanxdx.

(a) Let u=xu = xu=x and dv=e−x dx.dv = e^{-x}\,dx\mathclose{\text{.}}dv=e−xdx. Then du=dxdu = dxdu=dx and v=−e−x;v = -e^{-x}\mathclose{\text{;}}v=−e−x; any antiderivative of e−xe^{-x}e−x will do, so take the simplest. So

∫xe−x dx=x(−e−x)−∫(−e−x) dx=−xe−x+∫e−x dx=−xe−x−e−x+C.\begin{aligned} &\int xe^{-x}\,dx \\ &\quad= x\big(-e^{-x}\big) - \int \big(-e^{-x}\big)\,dx \\ &\quad= -xe^{-x} + \int e^{-x}\,dx \\ &\quad= -xe^{-x} - e^{-x} + C. \end{aligned}​∫xe−xdx=x(−e−x)−∫(−e−x)dx=−xe−x+∫e−xdx=−xe−x−e−x+C.​

Check: ddx(−xe−x−e−x)=−e−x+xe−x+e−x=xe−x.\dfrac{d}{dx}\big(-xe^{-x} - e^{-x}\big) = -e^{-x} + xe^{-x} + e^{-x} = xe^{-x}\mathclose{\text{.}}dxd​(−xe−x−e−x)=−e−x+xe−x+e−x=xe−x.

(b) There seems to be only one factor, but ln⁡x dx\ln x\,dxlnxdx is u dvu\,dvudv with u=ln⁡xu = \ln xu=lnx and dv=dx.dv = dx\mathclose{\text{.}}dv=dx. Then du=dxxdu = \dfrac{dx}{x}du=xdx​ and v=x:v = x\mathclose{\text{:}}v=x:

∫ln⁡x dx=xln⁡x−∫x⋅1x dx=xln⁡x−x+C.\begin{aligned} \int \ln x\,dx &= x\ln x - \int x\cdot\frac1x\,dx \\ &= x\ln x - x + C. \end{aligned}∫lnxdx​=xlnx−∫x⋅x1​dx=xlnx−x+C.​

(c) The same trick: u=arctan⁡xu = \arctan xu=arctanx and dv=dx,dv = dx\mathclose{\text{,}}dv=dx, so du=dx1+x2du = \dfrac{dx}{1 + x^2}du=1+x2dx​ and v=x.v = x\mathclose{\text{.}}v=x. Then

∫arctan⁡x dx=xarctan⁡x−∫x1+x2 dx=xarctan⁡x−12ln⁡(1+x2)+C,\begin{aligned} &\int \arctan x\,dx \\ &\quad= x\arctan x - \int \frac{x}{1 + x^2}\,dx \\ &\quad= x\arctan x - \tfrac12\ln\big(1 + x^2\big) + C, \end{aligned}​∫arctanxdx=xarctanx−∫1+x2x​dx=xarctanx−21​ln(1+x2)+C,​

the last integral by the substitution w=1+x2,w = 1 + x^2\mathclose{\text{,}}w=1+x2, dw=2x dxdw = 2x\,dxdw=2xdx (Module 10), with no absolute value bars because 1+x2>0.1 + x^2 > 0\mathclose{\text{.}}1+x2>0.

Choosing u and dv

The choice matters. In ∫xcos⁡x dx,\int x\cos x\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}∫xcosxdx, take the opposite roles, u=cos⁡xu = \cos xu=cosx and dv=x dx.dv = x\,dx\mathclose{\text{.}}dv=xdx. Then du=−sin⁡x dxdu = -\sin x\,dxdu=−sinxdx and v=12x2,v = \tfrac12x^2\mathclose{\text{,}}v=21​x2, and

∫xcos⁡x dx=12x2cos⁡x+12∫x2sin⁡x dx.\int x\cos x\,dx = \tfrac12x^2\cos x + \tfrac12\int x^2\sin x\,dx.∫xcosxdx=21​x2cosx+21​∫x2sinxdx.

That is true, but the new integral is harder than the old one: the power of xxx went up instead of down. Integration by parts pays off when differentiating uuu makes it simpler, and integrating dvdvdv does not make it much worse.

Key idea

A rough guide to the choice of uuu is the word LIATE. Take for uuu the factor whose kind comes first in the list

  1. Logarithmic: ln⁡x\ln xlnx
  2. Inverse trigonometric: arctan⁡x,\arctan x\mathclose{\text{,}}arctanx, arcsin⁡x\arcsin xarcsinx
  3. Algebraic: powers and polynomials, such as x,x\mathclose{\text{,}}x, x3,x^3\mathclose{\text{,}}x3, x\sqrt xx​
  4. Trigonometric: sin⁡x,\sin x\mathclose{\text{,}}sinx, cos⁡x\cos xcosx
  5. Exponential: ex,e^x\mathclose{\text{,}}ex, e−2x,e^{-2x}\mathclose{\text{,}}e−2x, 2x2^x2x

and let dvdvdv be the rest, with dx.dx\mathclose{\text{.}}dx. The kinds early in the list get simpler when they are differentiated (ln⁡x\ln xlnx becomes 1/x,1/x\mathclose{\text{,}}1/x, arctan⁡x\arctan xarctanx becomes 1/(1+x2),1/(1 + x^2)\mathclose{\text{,}}1/(1+x2), x3x^3x3 becomes 3x2);3x^2\mathclose{\text{);}}3x2); the kinds late in the list are easy to integrate and stay the same kind.

In ∫xe−x dx,\int xe^{-x}\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}∫xe−xdx, algebraic comes before exponential, so u=x;u = x\mathclose{\text{;}}u=x; in ∫ln⁡x dx\int \ln x\,dx∫lnxdx and ∫arctan⁡x dx,\int \arctan x\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}∫arctanxdx, the logarithm and the inverse tangent come first, and dv=dx.dv = dx\mathclose{\text{.}}dv=dx. But LIATE is a rule of thumb, not a theorem, and the requirement that you can integrate dvdvdv comes first.

Example 11.2When the guide misleads✓ Checked

Find ∫x3ex2 dx.\displaystyle\int x^3e^{x^2}\,dx\mathclose{\text{.}}∫x3ex2dx.

LIATE suggests u=x3u = x^3u=x3 and dv=ex2 dx.dv = e^{x^2}\,dx\mathclose{\text{.}}dv=ex2dx. But then vvv would be an antiderivative of ex2,e^{x^2}\mathclose{\text{,}}ex2, and no formula built from the functions of Module 1’s catalogue is one (Section 11.6). Split the integrand differently. The factor ex2e^{x^2}ex2 can be integrated only together with a factor x,x\mathclose{\text{,}}x, by the substitution w=x2,w = x^2\mathclose{\text{,}}w=x2, dw=2x dx:dw = 2x\,dx\mathclose{\text{:}}dw=2xdx: ∫xex2 dx=12ex2+C.\int xe^{x^2}\,dx = \tfrac12e^{x^2} + C\mathclose{\text{.}}∫xex2dx=21​ex2+C. So take

u=x2,dv=xex2 dx,du=2x dx,v=12ex2.\begin{aligned} u &= x^2, & dv &= xe^{x^2}\,dx, \\ du &= 2x\,dx, & v &= \tfrac12e^{x^2}. \end{aligned}udu​=x2,=2xdx,​dvv​=xex2dx,=21​ex2.​

Then

∫x3ex2 dx=12x2ex2−∫12ex2⋅2x dx=12x2ex2−12ex2+C=12(x2−1)ex2+C,\begin{aligned} \int x^3e^{x^2}\,dx &= \tfrac12x^2e^{x^2} - \int \tfrac12e^{x^2}\cdot 2x\,dx \\ &= \tfrac12x^2e^{x^2} - \tfrac12e^{x^2} + C \\ &= \tfrac12\big(x^2 - 1\big)e^{x^2} + C, \end{aligned}∫x3ex2dx​=21​x2ex2−∫21​ex2⋅2xdx=21​x2ex2−21​ex2+C=21​(x2−1)ex2+C,​

the middle integral by the same substitution. Check: ddx(12(x2−1)ex2)=xex2+12(x2−1)2xex2=x3ex2.\dfrac{d}{dx}\Big(\tfrac12\big(x^2 - 1\big)e^{x^2}\Big) = xe^{x^2} + \tfrac12\big(x^2 - 1\big)2xe^{x^2} = x^3e^{x^2}\mathclose{\text{.}}dxd​(21​(x2−1)ex2)=xex2+21​(x2−1)2xex2=x3ex2.

Watch out

Three slips with parts. (1) The sign: ∫u dv\int u\,dv∫udv is uvuvuv minus ∫v du.\int v\,du\mathclose{\text{.}}∫vdu. (2) Integrating dvdvdv carelessly. In ∫xe3x dx,\int xe^{3x}\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}∫xe3xdx, with u=xu = xu=x and dv=e3x dx,dv = e^{3x}\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}dv=e3xdx, vvv is 13e3x,\tfrac13e^{3x}\mathclose{\text{,}}31​e3x, not e3x,e^{3x}\mathclose{\text{,}}e3x, and the answer is 13xe3x−19e3x+C;\tfrac13xe^{3x} - \tfrac19e^{3x} + C\mathclose{\text{;}}31​xe3x−91​e3x+C; with v=e3xv = e^{3x}v=e3x you would get xe3x−e3x,xe^{3x} - e^{3x}\mathclose{\text{,}}xe3x−e3x, whose derivative is 3xe3x−2e3x.3xe^{3x} - 2e^{3x}\mathclose{\text{.}}3xe3x−2e3x. (3) A choice that cannot work: a dvdvdv you cannot integrate, as in Example 11.2, or a uuu that does not get simpler. Differentiate the answer to catch all three.

Repeated parts and the tabular method

Sometimes the new integral is simpler but still a product, and a second round of parts finishes the job.

Example 11.3Twice by parts✓ Checked

Find ∫x2sin⁡x dx.\displaystyle\int x^2\sin x\,dx\mathclose{\text{.}}∫x2sinxdx.

By LIATE, u=x2u = x^2u=x2 and dv=sin⁡x dx,dv = \sin x\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}dv=sinxdx, so du=2x dxdu = 2x\,dxdu=2xdx and v=−cos⁡x:v = -\cos x\mathclose{\text{:}}v=−cosx:

∫x2sin⁡x dx=−x2cos⁡x+∫2xcos⁡x dx.\begin{aligned} &\int x^2\sin x\,dx \\ &\quad= -x^2\cos x + \int 2x\cos x\,dx. \end{aligned}​∫x2sinxdx=−x2cosx+∫2xcosxdx.​

The new integrand is again a product, with a lower power of x.x\mathclose{\text{.}}x. It is twice the integral found at the start of this section (by parts with u=xu = xu=x and dv=cos⁡x dx),dv = \cos x\,dx\mathclose{\text{),}}dv=cosxdx), that is, 2(xsin⁡x+cos⁡x)+C.2(x\sin x + \cos x) + C\mathclose{\text{.}}2(xsinx+cosx)+C. So

∫x2sin⁡x dx=−x2cos⁡x+2xsin⁡x+2cos⁡x+C.\begin{aligned} &\int x^2\sin x\,dx \\ &\quad= -x^2\cos x + 2x\sin x \\ &\qquad + 2\cos x + C. \end{aligned}​∫x2sinxdx=−x2cosx+2xsinx+2cosx+C.​

Each round lowers the power of xxx by one, so xnx^nxn needs nnn rounds.

When uuu is a polynomial, the rounds follow a pattern that a table organises: the tabular method. Write uuu and its successive derivatives in one column, down to 0, and the function in dvdvdv and its successive antiderivatives in the other. Multiply each entry of the left column by the entry one row lower in the right column, give the products the signs +,−,+,−,…+, -, +, -, \dots+,−,+,−,… in turn, and add them up.

Example 11.4The tabular method✓ Checked

Find ∫x3e2x dx.\displaystyle\int x^3e^{2x}\,dx\mathclose{\text{.}}∫x3e2xdx.

Differentiate x3x^3x3 until it becomes 0, and integrate e2xe^{2x}e2x as many times:

Sign Differentiate Integrate
+++ x3x^3x3 e2xe^{2x}e2x
−-− 3x23x^23x2 12e2x\tfrac12e^{2x}21​e2x
+++ 6x6x6x 14e2x\tfrac14e^{2x}41​e2x
−-− 666 18e2x\tfrac18e^{2x}81​e2x
000 116e2x\tfrac1{16}e^{2x}161​e2x

Multiplying along the diagonals, with the signs of the first column,

∫x3e2x dx=12x3e2x−34x2e2x+34xe2x−38e2x+C=18e2x(4x3−6x2+6x−3)+C.\begin{aligned} &\int x^3e^{2x}\,dx \\ &\quad= \tfrac12x^3e^{2x} - \tfrac34x^2e^{2x} \\ &\qquad + \tfrac34xe^{2x} - \tfrac38e^{2x} + C \\ &\quad= \tfrac18e^{2x}\big(4x^3 - 6x^2 + 6x - 3\big) + C. \end{aligned}​∫x3e2xdx=21​x3e2x−43​x2e2x+43​xe2x−83​e2x+C=81​e2x(4x3−6x2+6x−3)+C.​

Each diagonal is one round of parts. The first round gives x3⋅12e2x−∫3x2⋅12e2x dx:x^3\cdot\tfrac12e^{2x} - \int 3x^2\cdot\tfrac12e^{2x}\,dx\mathclose{\text{:}}x3⋅21​e2x−∫3x2⋅21​e2xdx: the first product, minus the integral of the next row’s two entries. That integral is treated the same way, with every sign reversed, and so on. The process stops when the left column reaches 0, because then the leftover integral is 0.

Definite integrals by parts

For a definite integral, evaluate uvuvuv between the limits.

Theorem 11.2Integration by parts in definite integrals

If fff and ggg have continuous derivatives on [a,b],[a, b]\mathclose{\text{,}}[a,b], then

∫abf(x) g′(x) dx=[f(x) g(x)]ab−∫abf′(x) g(x) dx.\begin{aligned} &\int_a^b f(x)\,g'(x)\,dx \\ &\quad= \big[f(x)\,g(x)\big]_a^b - \int_a^b f'(x)\,g(x)\,dx. \end{aligned}​∫ab​f(x)g′(x)dx=[f(x)g(x)]ab​−∫ab​f′(x)g(x)dx.​
Proof

The functions fg′fg'fg′ and f′gf'gf′g are continuous on [a,b],[a, b]\mathclose{\text{,}}[a,b], so both integrals exist. Let GGG be an antiderivative of f′gf'gf′g on [a,b].[a, b]\mathclose{\text{.}}[a,b]. By Theorem 11.1, fg−Gfg - Gfg−G is an antiderivative of fg′,fg'\mathclose{\text{,}}fg′, so by Part 2 of the Fundamental Theorem (Section 10.5) the left side is [fg−G]ab=[fg]ab−[G]ab,\big[fg - G\big]_a^b = \big[fg\big]_a^b - \big[G\big]_a^b\mathclose{\text{,}}[fg−G]ab​=[fg]ab​−[G]ab​, and [G]ab=∫abf′g dx,\big[G\big]_a^b = \int_a^b f'g\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}[G]ab​=∫ab​f′gdx, by Part 2 again.

∎

When u=f(x)u = f(x)u=f(x) and v=g(x)v = g(x)v=g(x) are never negative and both increase with x,x\mathclose{\text{,}}x, the theorem has a picture (Figure 11.1). As xxx runs from aaa to b,b\mathclose{\text{,}}b, the point (u,v)(u, v)(u,v) traces a curve from (u1,v1)(u_1, v_1)(u1​,v1​) to (u2,v2),(u_2, v_2)\mathclose{\text{,}}(u2​,v2​), where u1=f(a),u_1 = f(a)\mathclose{\text{,}}u1​=f(a), v1=g(a),v_1 = g(a)\mathclose{\text{,}}v1​=g(a), u2=f(b)u_2 = f(b)u2​=f(b) and v2=g(b).v_2 = g(b)\mathclose{\text{.}}v2​=g(b). The integral ∫v du=∫abg(x)f′(x) dx\int v\,du = \int_a^b g(x)f'(x)\,dx∫vdu=∫ab​g(x)f′(x)dx is the area between this curve and the uuu-axis, and ∫u dv=∫abf(x)g′(x) dx\int u\,dv = \int_a^b f(x)g'(x)\,dx∫udv=∫ab​f(x)g′(x)dx is the area between the curve and the vvv-axis. Together the two regions fill the rectangle u2v2u_2v_2u2​v2​ except for the rectangle u1v1:u_1v_1\mathclose{\text{:}}u1​v1​:

∫u dv+∫v du=u2v2−u1v1=[uv]ab,\int u\,dv + \int v\,du = u_2v_2 - u_1v_1 = \big[uv\big]_a^b,∫udv+∫vdu=u2​v2​−u1​v1​=[uv]ab​,

which is Theorem 11.2.

Example 11.5Definite integrals by parts✓ Checked

Evaluate (a) ∫1eln⁡x dx\displaystyle\int_1^e \ln x\,dx∫1e​lnxdx and (b) ∫0πxsin⁡x dx.\displaystyle\int_0^\pi x\sin x\,dx\mathclose{\text{.}}∫0π​xsinxdx.

(a) With u=ln⁡xu = \ln xu=lnx and dv=dx,dv = dx\mathclose{\text{,}}dv=dx, as in Example 11.1(b),

∫1eln⁡x dx=[xln⁡x]1e−∫1ex⋅1x dx=(eln⁡e−1⋅ln⁡1)−(e−1)=e−(e−1)=1.\begin{aligned} &\int_1^e \ln x\,dx \\ &\quad= \big[x\ln x\big]_1^e - \int_1^e x\cdot\frac1x\,dx \\ &\quad= (e\ln e - 1\cdot\ln 1) - (e - 1) \\ &\quad= e - (e - 1) = 1. \end{aligned}​∫1e​lnxdx=[xlnx]1e​−∫1e​x⋅x1​dx=(elne−1⋅ln1)−(e−1)=e−(e−1)=1.​

Figure 11.1 (right) shows this area as the rectangle of area eee minus the region of area e−1e - 1e−1 to the left of the curve.

(b) With u=xu = xu=x and dv=sin⁡x dx,dv = \sin x\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}dv=sinxdx, so du=dxdu = dxdu=dx and v=−cos⁡x,v = -\cos x\mathclose{\text{,}}v=−cosx,

∫0πxsin⁡x dx=[−xcos⁡x]0π+∫0πcos⁡x dx=(−πcos⁡π+0)+[sin⁡x]0π=π+0=π.\begin{aligned} &\int_0^\pi x\sin x\,dx \\ &\quad= \big[-x\cos x\big]_0^\pi + \int_0^\pi \cos x\,dx \\ &\quad= (-\pi\cos\pi + 0) + \big[\sin x\big]_0^\pi \\ &\quad= \pi + 0 = \pi. \end{aligned}​∫0π​xsinxdx=[−xcosx]0π​+∫0π​cosxdx=(−πcosπ+0)+[sinx]0π​=π+0=π.​

When the integral comes back

In some integrals neither factor gets simpler when differentiated. Then two rounds of parts may bring back the integral you started with, and you can solve for it.

Example 11.6An integral that comes back✓ Checked

Find ∫exsin⁡x dx.\displaystyle\int e^x\sin x\,dx\mathclose{\text{.}}∫exsinxdx.

Call the integral I.I\mathclose{\text{.}}I. Take u=sin⁡xu = \sin xu=sinx and dv=ex dx,dv = e^x\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}dv=exdx, so du=cos⁡x dxdu = \cos x\,dxdu=cosxdx and v=ex:v = e^x\mathclose{\text{:}}v=ex:

I=exsin⁡x−∫excos⁡x dx.I = e^x\sin x - \int e^x\cos x\,dx.I=exsinx−∫excosxdx.

The new integral is of the same kind. Integrate by parts again, with the factors in the same roles, u=cos⁡xu = \cos xu=cosx and dv=ex dx,dv = e^x\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}dv=exdx, so du=−sin⁡x dx:du = -\sin x\,dx\mathclose{\text{:}}du=−sinxdx:

∫excos⁡x dx=excos⁡x+∫exsin⁡x dx=excos⁡x+I.\begin{aligned} &\int e^x\cos x\,dx \\ &\quad= e^x\cos x + \int e^x\sin x\,dx \\ &\quad= e^x\cos x + I. \end{aligned}​∫excosxdx=excosx+∫exsinxdx=excosx+I.​

Put this into the first equation:

I=exsin⁡x−excos⁡x−I.I = e^x\sin x - e^x\cos x - I.I=exsinx−excosx−I.

The unknown integral appears on both sides, so solve for it as in an equation: 2I=ex(sin⁡x−cos⁡x),2I = e^x(\sin x - \cos x)\mathclose{\text{,}}2I=ex(sinx−cosx), and

∫exsin⁡x dx=12ex(sin⁡x−cos⁡x)+C.\int e^x\sin x\,dx = \tfrac12e^x(\sin x - \cos x) + C.∫exsinxdx=21​ex(sinx−cosx)+C.

Each indefinite integral stands for a family of functions that differ by constants, so these equations hold up to constants; the + C+\,C+C at the end collects them. Check: ddx(12ex(sin⁡x−cos⁡x))=12ex(sin⁡x−cos⁡x)+12ex(cos⁡x+sin⁡x)=exsin⁡x.\dfrac{d}{dx}\Big(\tfrac12e^x(\sin x - \cos x)\Big) = \tfrac12e^x(\sin x - \cos x) + \tfrac12e^x(\cos x + \sin x) = e^x\sin x\mathclose{\text{.}}dxd​(21​ex(sinx−cosx))=21​ex(sinx−cosx)+21​ex(cosx+sinx)=exsinx.

Watch out

In the second round, keep the roles of the first. With u=exu = e^xu=ex and dv=cos⁡x dxdv = \cos x\,dxdv=cosxdx instead, the second round undoes the first: ∫excos⁡x dx=exsin⁡x−I,\int e^x\cos x\,dx = e^x\sin x - I\mathclose{\text{,}}∫excosxdx=exsinx−I, and the first equation becomes I=exsin⁡x−exsin⁡x+I,I = e^x\sin x - e^x\sin x + I\mathclose{\text{,}}I=exsinx−exsinx+I, that is, I=I.I = I\mathclose{\text{.}}I=I. True, but no help.

Reduction formulas

Some integrals depend on a whole number n,n\mathclose{\text{,}}n, such as ∫sin⁡nx dx\int \sin^n x\,dx∫sinnxdx or ∫xnex dx.\int x^ne^x\,dx\mathclose{\text{.}}∫xnexdx. Integration by parts can lower n.n\mathclose{\text{.}}n. A reduction formula expresses such an integral in terms of the same integral with a smaller n;n\mathclose{\text{;}}n; applied again and again, it brings nnn down to 0 or 1.

Theorem 11.3A reduction formula for powers of sine

For every whole number n≥2,n \ge 2\mathclose{\text{,}}n≥2,

∫sin⁡nx dx=−sin⁡n−1xcos⁡xn+n−1n∫sin⁡n−2x dx.\begin{aligned} \int \sin^n x\,dx &= -\frac{\sin^{n-1}x\cos x}{n} \\ &\quad + \frac{n - 1}{n}\int \sin^{n-2}x\,dx. \end{aligned}∫sinnxdx​=−nsinn−1xcosx​+nn−1​∫sinn−2xdx.​
Proof

Write sin⁡nx=sin⁡n−1x⋅sin⁡x\sin^n x = \sin^{n-1}x\cdot\sin xsinnx=sinn−1x⋅sinx and integrate by parts with u=sin⁡n−1xu = \sin^{n-1}xu=sinn−1x and dv=sin⁡x dx.dv = \sin x\,dx\mathclose{\text{.}}dv=sinxdx. By the chain rule du=(n−1)sin⁡n−2xcos⁡x dx,du = (n - 1)\sin^{n-2}x\cos x\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}du=(n−1)sinn−2xcosxdx, and v=−cos⁡x:v = -\cos x\mathclose{\text{:}}v=−cosx:

∫sin⁡nx dx=−sin⁡n−1xcos⁡x+(n−1)∫sin⁡n−2xcos⁡2x dx.\begin{aligned} &\int \sin^n x\,dx \\ &\quad= -\sin^{n-1}x\cos x \\ &\qquad + (n - 1)\int \sin^{n-2}x\cos^2 x\,dx. \end{aligned}​∫sinnxdx=−sinn−1xcosx+(n−1)∫sinn−2xcos2xdx.​

Replace cos⁡2x\cos^2 xcos2x by 1−sin⁡2x1 - \sin^2 x1−sin2x and split the integral:

∫sin⁡nx dx=−sin⁡n−1xcos⁡x+(n−1)∫sin⁡n−2x dx−(n−1)∫sin⁡nx dx.\begin{aligned} &\int \sin^n x\,dx \\ &\quad= -\sin^{n-1}x\cos x \\ &\qquad + (n - 1)\int \sin^{n-2}x\,dx \\ &\qquad - (n - 1)\int \sin^n x\,dx. \end{aligned}​∫sinnxdx=−sinn−1xcosx+(n−1)∫sinn−2xdx−(n−1)∫sinnxdx.​

The integral of sin⁡nx\sin^n xsinnx has come back, as in Example 11.6. Add (n−1)∫sin⁡nx dx(n - 1)\int \sin^n x\,dx(n−1)∫sinnxdx to both sides and divide by n.n\mathclose{\text{.}}n.

∎
Example 11.7Powers of sine✓ Checked

Find (a) ∫sin⁡2x dx,\displaystyle\int \sin^2 x\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}∫sin2xdx, (b) ∫sin⁡4x dx\displaystyle\int \sin^4 x\,dx∫sin4xdx and (c) ∫0π/2sin⁡4x dx.\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^4 x\,dx\mathclose{\text{.}}∫0π/2​sin4xdx.

(a) With n=2,n = 2\mathclose{\text{,}}n=2, and sin⁡0x=1,\sin^0 x = 1\mathclose{\text{,}}sin0x=1,

∫sin⁡2x dx=−12sin⁡xcos⁡x+12x+C.\int \sin^2 x\,dx = -\tfrac12\sin x\cos x + \tfrac12x + C.∫sin2xdx=−21​sinxcosx+21​x+C.

(b) With n=4,n = 4\mathclose{\text{,}}n=4, and then (a),

∫sin⁡4x dx=−14sin⁡3xcos⁡x+34∫sin⁡2x dx=−14sin⁡3xcos⁡x−38sin⁡xcos⁡x+38x+C.\begin{aligned} &\int \sin^4 x\,dx \\ &\quad= -\tfrac14\sin^3 x\cos x + \tfrac34\int \sin^2 x\,dx \\ &\quad= -\tfrac14\sin^3 x\cos x - \tfrac38\sin x\cos x \\ &\qquad + \tfrac38x + C. \end{aligned}​∫sin4xdx=−41​sin3xcosx+43​∫sin2xdx=−41​sin3xcosx−83​sinxcosx+83​x+C.​

(c) In a definite integral, the reduction formula holds with its first term evaluated between the limits (use Theorem 11.2 in the proof). On [0,π/2][0, \pi/2][0,π/2] that term vanishes at both ends, since sin⁡0=0,\sin 0 = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}sin0=0, cos⁡π2=0\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2} = 0cos2π​=0 and the power n−1n - 1n−1 is at least 1. So, applying the formula twice,

∫0π/2sin⁡4x dx=34∫0π/2sin⁡2x dx=34⋅12∫0π/21 dx=34⋅12⋅π2=3π16≈0.5890.\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^4 x\,dx &= \frac34\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^2 x\,dx \\ &= \frac34\cdot\frac12\int_0^{\pi/2} 1\,dx \\ &= \frac34\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} \\ &= \frac{3\pi}{16} \approx 0.5890. \end{aligned}∫0π/2​sin4xdx​=43​∫0π/2​sin2xdx=43​⋅21​∫0π/2​1dx=43​⋅21​⋅2π​=163π​≈0.5890.​

The second line says that ∫0π/2sin⁡2x dx=12⋅π2=π4,\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^2 x\,dx = \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{2} = \tfrac{\pi}{4}\mathclose{\text{,}}∫0π/2​sin2xdx=21​⋅2π​=4π​, as Exercise 10.12 found by symmetry.

Trigonometric integrals

Example 11.7 integrated powers of the sine with a reduction formula. Most products of powers of sines and cosines give way faster, to an identity and a substitution. Three identities do the work. The first is the Pythagorean identity sin⁡2x+cos⁡2x=1\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1sin2x+cos2x=1 of Module 1; dividing it by cos⁡2x\cos^2 xcos2x gives the second, tan⁡2x+1=sec⁡2x.\tan^2 x + 1 = \sec^2 x\mathclose{\text{.}}tan2x+1=sec2x. The third comes from the addition formula cos⁡(x+y)=cos⁡xcos⁡y−sin⁡xsin⁡y\cos(x + y) = \cos x\cos y - \sin x\sin ycos(x+y)=cosxcosy−sinxsiny of Module 1, with y=x:y = x\mathclose{\text{:}}y=x:

cos⁡2x=cos⁡2x−sin⁡2x.\cos 2x = \cos^2 x - \sin^2 x.cos2x=cos2x−sin2x.

Replacing cos⁡2x\cos^2 xcos2x by 1−sin⁡2x,1 - \sin^2 x\mathclose{\text{,}}1−sin2x, or sin⁡2x\sin^2 xsin2x by 1−cos⁡2x,1 - \cos^2 x\mathclose{\text{,}}1−cos2x, and solving gives the half-angle identities

sin⁡2x=1−cos⁡2x2,cos⁡2x=1+cos⁡2x2.\begin{aligned} \sin^2 x &= \frac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}, \\ \cos^2 x &= \frac{1 + \cos 2x}{2}. \end{aligned}sin2xcos2x​=21−cos2x​,=21+cos2x​.​

They trade a square for a cosine of twice the angle, which is easy to integrate. In the same way the addition formula for the sine gives sin⁡2x=2sin⁡xcos⁡x.\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos x\mathclose{\text{.}}sin2x=2sinxcosx.

Powers of sine and cosine

Key idea

To integrate sin⁡mxcos⁡nx,\sin^m x\cos^n x\mathclose{\text{,}}sinmxcosnx, where mmm and nnn are whole numbers:

  • If the power nnn of the cosine is odd, save one factor cos⁡x,\cos x\mathclose{\text{,}}cosx, write the remaining even power of the cosine in terms of the sine with cos⁡2x=1−sin⁡2x,\cos^2 x = 1 - \sin^2 x\mathclose{\text{,}}cos2x=1−sin2x, and substitute u=sin⁡x,u = \sin x\mathclose{\text{,}}u=sinx, du=cos⁡x dx.du = \cos x\,dx\mathclose{\text{.}}du=cosxdx.
  • If the power mmm of the sine is odd, save one factor sin⁡x,\sin x\mathclose{\text{,}}sinx, use sin⁡2x=1−cos⁡2x,\sin^2 x = 1 - \cos^2 x\mathclose{\text{,}}sin2x=1−cos2x, and substitute u=cos⁡x,u = \cos x\mathclose{\text{,}}u=cosx, du=−sin⁡x dx.du = -\sin x\,dx\mathclose{\text{.}}du=−sinxdx.
  • If both powers are even, use the half-angle identities, again and again if needed, or the reduction formula of Theorem 11.3.
Example 11.8Odd powers✓ Checked

Find (a) ∫sin⁡3x dx\displaystyle\int \sin^3 x\,dx∫sin3xdx and (b) ∫sin⁡2xcos⁡3x dx.\displaystyle\int \sin^2 x\cos^3 x\,dx\mathclose{\text{.}}∫sin2xcos3xdx.

(a) The power of the sine is odd. Save one sin⁡x:\sin x\mathclose{\text{:}}sinx: sin⁡3x=sin⁡2x⋅sin⁡x=(1−cos⁡2x)sin⁡x.\sin^3 x = \sin^2 x\cdot\sin x = \big(1 - \cos^2 x\big)\sin x\mathclose{\text{.}}sin3x=sin2x⋅sinx=(1−cos2x)sinx. With u=cos⁡xu = \cos xu=cosx and du=−sin⁡x dx,du = -\sin x\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}du=−sinxdx,

∫sin⁡3x dx=−∫(1−u2) du=−u+u33+C=−cos⁡x+13cos⁡3x+C.\begin{aligned} \int \sin^3 x\,dx &= -\int \big(1 - u^2\big)\,du \\ &= -u + \frac{u^3}{3} + C \\ &= -\cos x + \tfrac13\cos^3 x + C. \end{aligned}∫sin3xdx​=−∫(1−u2)du=−u+3u3​+C=−cosx+31​cos3x+C.​

(b) The power of the cosine is odd. Save one cos⁡x:\cos x\mathclose{\text{:}}cosx: sin⁡2xcos⁡3x=sin⁡2x(1−sin⁡2x)cos⁡x.\sin^2 x\cos^3 x = \sin^2 x\big(1 - \sin^2 x\big)\cos x\mathclose{\text{.}}sin2xcos3x=sin2x(1−sin2x)cosx. With u=sin⁡xu = \sin xu=sinx and du=cos⁡x dx,du = \cos x\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}du=cosxdx,

∫sin⁡2xcos⁡3x dx=∫(u2−u4) du=13sin⁡3x−15sin⁡5x+C.\begin{aligned} &\int \sin^2 x\cos^3 x\,dx \\ &\quad= \int \big(u^2 - u^4\big)\,du \\ &\quad= \tfrac13\sin^3 x - \tfrac15\sin^5 x + C. \end{aligned}​∫sin2xcos3xdx=∫(u2−u4)du=31​sin3x−51​sin5x+C.​
Example 11.9Even powers✓ Checked

Find (a) ∫cos⁡2x dx\displaystyle\int \cos^2 x\,dx∫cos2xdx and (b) ∫0πsin⁡4x dx.\displaystyle\int_0^\pi \sin^4 x\,dx\mathclose{\text{.}}∫0π​sin4xdx.

(a) By the half-angle identity, and with ∫cos⁡2x dx=12sin⁡2x+C\int \cos 2x\,dx = \tfrac12\sin 2x + C∫cos2xdx=21​sin2x+C from Module 10’s table,

∫cos⁡2x dx=12∫(1+cos⁡2x) dx=x2+sin⁡2x4+C.\begin{aligned} \int \cos^2 x\,dx &= \frac12\int (1 + \cos 2x)\,dx \\ &= \frac{x}{2} + \frac{\sin 2x}{4} + C. \end{aligned}∫cos2xdx​=21​∫(1+cos2x)dx=2x​+4sin2x​+C.​

(b) Square the half-angle identity for sin⁡2x,\sin^2 x\mathclose{\text{,}}sin2x, then use the one for cos⁡2\cos^2cos2 again, with 2x2x2x in place of x:x\mathclose{\text{:}}x:

sin⁡4x=(1−cos⁡2x2)2=14(1−2cos⁡2x+cos⁡22x)=14(1−2cos⁡2x+1+cos⁡4x2)=38−12cos⁡2x+18cos⁡4x.\begin{aligned} \sin^4 x &= \Big(\frac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}\Big)^2 \\ &= \frac14\big(1 - 2\cos 2x + \cos^2 2x\big) \\ &= \frac14\Big(1 - 2\cos 2x + \frac{1 + \cos 4x}{2}\Big) \\ &= \frac38 - \frac12\cos 2x + \frac18\cos 4x. \end{aligned}sin4x​=(21−cos2x​)2=41​(1−2cos2x+cos22x)=41​(1−2cos2x+21+cos4x​)=83​−21​cos2x+81​cos4x.​

So

∫0πsin⁡4x dx=[3x8−sin⁡2x4+sin⁡4x32]0π=3π8≈1.178,\begin{aligned} &\int_0^\pi \sin^4 x\,dx \\ &\quad= \Big[\frac{3x}{8} - \frac{\sin 2x}{4} + \frac{\sin 4x}{32}\Big]_0^\pi \\ &\quad= \frac{3\pi}{8} \approx 1.178, \end{aligned}​∫0π​sin4xdx=[83x​−4sin2x​+32sin4x​]0π​=83π​≈1.178,​

since all the sines vanish at 0 and at π.\pi\mathclose{\text{.}}π. This is twice the value 3π16\tfrac{3\pi}{16}163π​ found on [0,π/2][0, \pi/2][0,π/2] in Example 11.7, as it should be: the graph of sin⁡4x\sin^4 xsin4x is symmetric about x=π/2,x = \pi/2\mathclose{\text{,}}x=π/2, because sin⁡(π−x)=sin⁡x.\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x\mathclose{\text{.}}sin(π−x)=sinx.

Watch out

Three slips. (1) sin⁡2x\sin^2 xsin2x is (sin⁡x)2,(\sin x)^2\mathclose{\text{,}}(sinx)2, not sin⁡(x2).\sin(x^2)\mathclose{\text{.}}sin(x2). (2) The power rule does not apply to sin⁡2x\sin^2 xsin2x as if sin⁡x\sin xsinx were x:x\mathclose{\text{:}}x: ∫sin⁡2x dx\int \sin^2 x\,dx∫sin2xdx is not 13sin⁡3x+C,\tfrac13\sin^3 x + C\mathclose{\text{,}}31​sin3x+C, whose derivative is sin⁡2xcos⁡x\sin^2 x\cos xsin2xcosx by the chain rule. (3) ∫cos⁡2x dx=12sin⁡2x+C,\int \cos 2x\,dx = \tfrac12\sin 2x + C\mathclose{\text{,}}∫cos2xdx=21​sin2x+C, not sin⁡2x+C;\sin 2x + C\mathclose{\text{;}}sin2x+C; and cos⁡2x\cos 2xcos2x is not 2cos⁡x.2\cos x\mathclose{\text{.}}2cosx.

Powers of tangent and secant

For tangents and secants the derivatives (tan⁡x)′=sec⁡2x(\tan x)' = \sec^2 x(tanx)′=sec2x and (sec⁡x)′=sec⁡xtan⁡x(\sec x)' = \sec x\tan x(secx)′=secxtanx of Module 5 play the parts of cos⁡x\cos xcosx and sin⁡x,\sin x\mathclose{\text{,}}sinx, and sec⁡2x=1+tan⁡2x\sec^2 x = 1 + \tan^2 xsec2x=1+tan2x plays the part of the Pythagorean identity.

Key idea

To integrate tan⁡mxsec⁡nx,\tan^m x\sec^n x\mathclose{\text{,}}tanmxsecnx, where mmm and nnn are whole numbers:

  • If the power nnn of the secant is even and at least 2, save sec⁡2x,\sec^2 x\mathclose{\text{,}}sec2x, write the other secants in terms of the tangent with sec⁡2x=1+tan⁡2x,\sec^2 x = 1 + \tan^2 x\mathclose{\text{,}}sec2x=1+tan2x, and substitute u=tan⁡x,u = \tan x\mathclose{\text{,}}u=tanx, du=sec⁡2x dx.du = \sec^2 x\,dx\mathclose{\text{.}}du=sec2xdx.
  • If the power mmm of the tangent is odd and n≥1,n \ge 1\mathclose{\text{,}}n≥1, save sec⁡xtan⁡x,\sec x\tan x\mathclose{\text{,}}secxtanx, write the other tangents in terms of the secant with tan⁡2x=sec⁡2x−1,\tan^2 x = \sec^2 x - 1\mathclose{\text{,}}tan2x=sec2x−1, and substitute u=sec⁡x,u = \sec x\mathclose{\text{,}}u=secx, du=sec⁡xtan⁡x dx.du = \sec x\tan x\,dx\mathclose{\text{.}}du=secxtanxdx.
  • Otherwise use identities, the integrals of tan⁡x\tan xtanx (Example 10.11) and sec⁡x\sec xsecx (Theorem 11.4), or parts (Example 11.11).
Example 11.10Tangents and secants✓ Checked

Find (a) ∫tan⁡2xsec⁡4x dx,\displaystyle\int \tan^2 x\sec^4 x\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}∫tan2xsec4xdx, (b) ∫tan⁡3xsec⁡x dx\displaystyle\int \tan^3 x\sec x\,dx∫tan3xsecxdx and (c) ∫tan⁡2x dx,\displaystyle\int \tan^2 x\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}∫tan2xdx, on an interval where cos⁡x≠0.\cos x \ne 0\mathclose{\text{.}}cosx=0.

(a) The power of the secant is even: tan⁡2xsec⁡4x=tan⁡2x(1+tan⁡2x)sec⁡2x.\tan^2 x\sec^4 x = \tan^2 x\big(1 + \tan^2 x\big)\sec^2 x\mathclose{\text{.}}tan2xsec4x=tan2x(1+tan2x)sec2x. With u=tan⁡x,u = \tan x\mathclose{\text{,}}u=tanx,

∫(u2+u4) du=13tan⁡3x+15tan⁡5x+C.\begin{aligned} &\int \big(u^2 + u^4\big)\,du \\ &\quad= \tfrac13\tan^3 x + \tfrac15\tan^5 x + C. \end{aligned}​∫(u2+u4)du=31​tan3x+51​tan5x+C.​

(b) The power of the tangent is odd: tan⁡3xsec⁡x=(sec⁡2x−1)sec⁡xtan⁡x.\tan^3 x\sec x = \big(\sec^2 x - 1\big)\sec x\tan x\mathclose{\text{.}}tan3xsecx=(sec2x−1)secxtanx. With u=sec⁡x,u = \sec x\mathclose{\text{,}}u=secx,

∫(u2−1) du=13sec⁡3x−sec⁡x+C.\int \big(u^2 - 1\big)\,du = \tfrac13\sec^3 x - \sec x + C.∫(u2−1)du=31​sec3x−secx+C.

(c) There is no secant, but the identity still helps:

∫tan⁡2x dx=∫(sec⁡2x−1) dx=tan⁡x−x+C.\begin{aligned} \int \tan^2 x\,dx &= \int \big(\sec^2 x - 1\big)\,dx \\ &= \tan x - x + C. \end{aligned}∫tan2xdx​=∫(sec2x−1)dx=tanx−x+C.​

The integral of sec⁡x\sec xsecx itself needs a trick.

Theorem 11.4The integral of the secant

On every interval on which cos⁡x≠0,\cos x \ne 0\mathclose{\text{,}}cosx=0,

∫sec⁡x dx=ln⁡∣sec⁡x+tan⁡x∣+C.\int \sec x\,dx = \ln\abs{\sec x + \tan x} + C.∫secxdx=ln∣secx+tanx∣+C.
Proof

Where cos⁡x≠0,\cos x \ne 0\mathclose{\text{,}}cosx=0, sec⁡x+tan⁡x=1+sin⁡xcos⁡x\sec x + \tan x = \dfrac{1 + \sin x}{\cos x}secx+tanx=cosx1+sinx​ is never 0: 1+sin⁡x=01 + \sin x = 01+sinx=0 would mean sin⁡x=−1,\sin x = -1\mathclose{\text{,}}sinx=−1, and then cos⁡x=0.\cos x = 0\mathclose{\text{.}}cosx=0. So ln⁡∣sec⁡x+tan⁡x∣\ln\abs{\sec x + \tan x}ln∣secx+tanx∣ is differentiable there, and by the chain rule, with ddxln⁡∣w∣=w′w\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln\abs{w} = \dfrac{w'}{w}dxd​ln∣w∣=ww′​ (Module 6),

ddxln⁡∣sec⁡x+tan⁡x∣=sec⁡xtan⁡x+sec⁡2xsec⁡x+tan⁡x=sec⁡x(tan⁡x+sec⁡x)sec⁡x+tan⁡x=sec⁡x.\begin{aligned} &\frac{d}{dx}\ln\abs{\sec x + \tan x} \\ &\quad= \frac{\sec x\tan x + \sec^2 x}{\sec x + \tan x} \\ &\quad= \frac{\sec x(\tan x + \sec x)}{\sec x + \tan x} = \sec x. \end{aligned}​dxd​ln∣secx+tanx∣=secx+tanxsecxtanx+sec2x​=secx+tanxsecx(tanx+secx)​=secx.​
∎

The proof checks the formula; it does not show how anyone could find it. Here is one way, with a trick: multiply the integrand by 1, in the form sec⁡x+tan⁡xsec⁡x+tan⁡x.\dfrac{\sec x + \tan x}{\sec x + \tan x}\mathclose{\text{.}}secx+tanxsecx+tanx​. Then

∫sec⁡x dx=∫sec⁡2x+sec⁡xtan⁡xsec⁡x+tan⁡x dx,\int \sec x\,dx = \int \frac{\sec^2 x + \sec x\tan x}{\sec x + \tan x}\,dx,∫secxdx=∫secx+tanxsec2x+secxtanx​dx,

and the numerator is the derivative of the denominator, so the substitution w=sec⁡x+tan⁡xw = \sec x + \tan xw=secx+tanx gives ∫dww=ln⁡∣w∣+C.\int \dfrac{dw}{w} = \ln\abs{w} + C\mathclose{\text{.}}∫wdw​=ln∣w∣+C. Tricks like this one come from experience, which is one reason to check every antiderivative by differentiating it. The same trick with csc⁡x−cot⁡x,\csc x - \cot x\mathclose{\text{,}}cscx−cotx, whose derivative is csc⁡2x−csc⁡xcot⁡x,\csc^2 x - \csc x\cot x\mathclose{\text{,}}csc2x−cscxcotx, gives ∫csc⁡x dx=ln⁡∣csc⁡x−cot⁡x∣+C\int \csc x\,dx = \ln\abs{\csc x - \cot x} + C∫cscxdx=ln∣cscx−cotx∣+C on every interval on which sin⁡x≠0.\sin x \ne 0\mathclose{\text{.}}sinx=0.

Example 11.11The secant cubed✓ Checked

Find ∫sec⁡3x dx\displaystyle\int \sec^3 x\,dx∫sec3xdx on an interval where cos⁡x≠0.\cos x \ne 0\mathclose{\text{.}}cosx=0.

The power of the secant is odd and there is no tangent, so neither substitution applies. Integrate by parts with u=sec⁡xu = \sec xu=secx and dv=sec⁡2x dx,dv = \sec^2 x\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}dv=sec2xdx, so du=sec⁡xtan⁡x dxdu = \sec x\tan x\,dxdu=secxtanxdx and v=tan⁡x:v = \tan x\mathclose{\text{:}}v=tanx:

∫sec⁡3x dx=sec⁡xtan⁡x−∫sec⁡xtan⁡2x dx=sec⁡xtan⁡x−∫sec⁡x(sec⁡2x−1) dx=sec⁡xtan⁡x−∫sec⁡3x dx+∫sec⁡x dx.\begin{aligned} &\int \sec^3 x\,dx \\ &\quad= \sec x\tan x - \int \sec x\tan^2 x\,dx \\ &\quad= \sec x\tan x \\ &\qquad - \int \sec x\big(\sec^2 x - 1\big)\,dx \\ &\quad= \sec x\tan x - \int \sec^3 x\,dx \\ &\qquad + \int \sec x\,dx. \end{aligned}​∫sec3xdx=secxtanx−∫secxtan2xdx=secxtanx−∫secx(sec2x−1)dx=secxtanx−∫sec3xdx+∫secxdx.​

∫sec⁡3x dx=12sec⁡xtan⁡x+12ln⁡∣sec⁡x+tan⁡x∣+C.\begin{aligned} &\int \sec^3 x\,dx \\ &\quad= \tfrac12\sec x\tan x \\ &\qquad + \tfrac12\ln\abs{\sec x + \tan x} + C. \end{aligned}​∫sec3xdx=21​secxtanx+21​ln∣secx+tanx∣+C.​

Trigonometric substitution

The area of a disc of radius rrr is πr2,\pi r^2\mathclose{\text{,}}πr2, and Module 9 used that formula to evaluate integrals such as ∫039−x2 dx\int_0^3 \sqrt{9 - x^2}\,dx∫03​9−x2​dx (Exercise 9.4). Now integration can find such areas itself. The upper half of the circle x2+y2=r2x^2 + y^2 = r^2x2+y2=r2 is the graph of y=r2−x2,y = \sqrt{r^2 - x^2}\mathclose{\text{,}}y=r2−x2​, but no substitution u=g(x)u = g(x)u=g(x) of Module 10 helps with this integrand: there is no factor g′(x)g'(x)g′(x) to go with dx.dx\mathclose{\text{.}}dx. Instead, go the other way, and replace xxx by a function of a new variable. Since 1−sin⁡2θ=cos⁡2θ,1 - \sin^2\theta = \cos^2\theta\mathclose{\text{,}}1−sin2θ=cos2θ, the substitution x=rsin⁡θx = r\sin\thetax=rsinθ turns r2−x2\sqrt{r^2 - x^2}r2−x2​ into r2cos⁡2θ,\sqrt{r^2\cos^2\theta}\mathclose{\text{,}}r2cos2θ​, a square root that goes away.

The substitution rule of Module 10 justifies this, read from right to left.

Theorem 11.5Substitution in reverse

Let ggg have a continuous derivative on an interval J.J\mathclose{\text{.}}J.

  • (a) If fff is continuous on an interval that contains every value of ggg on J,J\mathclose{\text{,}}J, then for all α\alphaα and β\betaβ in JJJ
    ∫g(α)g(β)f(x) dx=∫αβf(g(θ)) g′(θ) dθ.\begin{aligned} &\int_{g(\alpha)}^{g(\beta)} f(x)\,dx \\ &\quad= \int_\alpha^\beta f\big(g(\theta)\big)\,g'(\theta)\,d\theta. \end{aligned}​∫g(α)g(β)​f(x)dx=∫αβ​f(g(θ))g′(θ)dθ.​
  • (b) Suppose that JJJ is open, that ggg is one-to-one on J,J\mathclose{\text{,}}J, that fff is continuous on the interval III of the values of ggg on J,J\mathclose{\text{,}}J, and that GGG is an antiderivative of f(g(θ)) g′(θ)f\big(g(\theta)\big)\,g'(\theta)f(g(θ))g′(θ) on J.J\mathclose{\text{.}}J. Then G(g−1(x))G\big(g^{-1}(x)\big)G(g−1(x)) is an antiderivative of fff on I.I\mathclose{\text{.}}I.
Proof

(a) is the substitution rule for definite integrals (Theorem 10.7), with x=g(θ),x = g(\theta)\mathclose{\text{,}}x=g(θ), read from right to left. For (b): III is an open interval, because ggg is continuous and one-to-one on the open interval J.J\mathclose{\text{.}}J. By Part 1 of the Fundamental Theorem, fff has an antiderivative FFF on I,I\mathclose{\text{,}}I, and by the substitution rule (Theorem 10.6), F(g(θ))F\big(g(\theta)\big)F(g(θ)) is an antiderivative of f(g(θ)) g′(θ)f\big(g(\theta)\big)\,g'(\theta)f(g(θ))g′(θ) on J.J\mathclose{\text{.}}J. So G(θ)=F(g(θ))+C0G(\theta) = F\big(g(\theta)\big) + C_0G(θ)=F(g(θ))+C0​ for a constant C0C_0C0​ (Theorem 10.1). For xxx in I,I\mathclose{\text{,}}I, put θ=g−1(x):\theta = g^{-1}(x)\mathclose{\text{:}}θ=g−1(x): then G(g−1(x))=F(x)+C0,G\big(g^{-1}(x)\big) = F(x) + C_0\mathclose{\text{,}}G(g−1(x))=F(x)+C0​, which is an antiderivative of f.f\mathclose{\text{.}}f.

Example 11.12The area of a circle and of an ellipse✓ Checked

Find the area enclosed by the circle x2+y2=r2,x^2 + y^2 = r^2\mathclose{\text{,}}x2+y2=r2, and by the ellipse x2a2+y2b2=1,\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\mathclose{\text{,}}a2x2​+b2y2​=1, where r,r\mathclose{\text{,}}r, aaa and bbb are positive.

The circle. The upper half of the disc is the region under the graph of y=r2−x2,y = \sqrt{r^2 - x^2}\mathclose{\text{,}}y=r2−x2​, for −r≤x≤r,-r \le x \le r\mathclose{\text{,}}−r≤x≤r, and the lower half is its mirror image in the xxx-axis. So the area of the disc is ∫−rr2r2−x2 dx.\int_{-r}^{r} 2\sqrt{r^2 - x^2}\,dx\mathclose{\text{.}}∫−rr​2r2−x2​dx. Substitute x=rsin⁡θx = r\sin\thetax=rsinθ with −π2≤θ≤π2.-\tfrac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}\mathclose{\text{.}}−2π​≤θ≤2π​. Then dx=rcos⁡θ dθ,dx = r\cos\theta\,d\theta\mathclose{\text{,}}dx=rcosθdθ, and r2−r2sin⁡2θ=r2cos⁡2θ=rcos⁡θ,\sqrt{r^2 - r^2\sin^2\theta} = \sqrt{r^2\cos^2\theta} = r\cos\theta\mathclose{\text{,}}r2−r2sin2θ​=r2cos2θ​=rcosθ, because cos⁡θ≥0\cos\theta \ge 0cosθ≥0 on this range. The limits x=−rx = -rx=−r and x=rx = rx=r correspond to θ=−π2\theta = -\tfrac{\pi}{2}θ=−2π​ and θ=π2.\theta = \tfrac{\pi}{2}\mathclose{\text{.}}θ=2π​. By Theorem 11.5(a) and Example 11.9(a),

∫−rr2r2−x2 dx=∫−π/2π/22rcos⁡θ⋅rcos⁡θ dθ=2r2∫−π/2π/2cos⁡2θ dθ=2r2[θ2+sin⁡2θ4]−π/2π/2=2r2⋅π2=πr2.\begin{aligned} &\int_{-r}^{r} 2\sqrt{r^2 - x^2}\,dx \\ &\quad= \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} 2r\cos\theta\cdot r\cos\theta\,d\theta \\ &\quad= 2r^2\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \cos^2\theta\,d\theta \\ &\quad= 2r^2\Big[\frac{\theta}{2} + \frac{\sin 2\theta}{4}\Big]_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \\ &\quad= 2r^2\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} = \pi r^2. \end{aligned}​∫−rr​2r2−x2​dx=∫−π/2π/2​2rcosθ⋅rcosθdθ=2r2∫−π/2π/2​cos2θdθ=2r2[2θ​+4sin2θ​]−π/2π/2​=2r2⋅2π​=πr2.​

The ellipse. Solving its equation for yyy gives y=±baa2−x2,y = \pm\tfrac{b}{a}\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}\mathclose{\text{,}}y=±ab​a2−x2​, for −a≤x≤a.-a \le x \le a\mathclose{\text{.}}−a≤x≤a. In the same way, the upper half of the region inside the ellipse lies under the graph of y=baa2−x2,y = \tfrac{b}{a}\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}\mathclose{\text{,}}y=ab​a2−x2​, and the lower half is its mirror image. So the area is ba\tfrac{b}{a}ab​ times that of the disc of radius a:a\mathclose{\text{:}}a:

ba∫−aa2a2−x2 dx=ba⋅πa2=πab.\frac{b}{a}\int_{-a}^{a} 2\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}\,dx = \frac{b}{a}\cdot\pi a^2 = \pi ab.ab​∫−aa​2a2−x2​dx=ab​⋅πa2=πab.

For a=b=ra = b = ra=b=r the ellipse is the circle, and πab=πr2,\pi ab = \pi r^2\mathclose{\text{,}}πab=πr2, as it should be.

Good to know

Example 11.12 does not prove from nothing that a disc has area πr2.\pi r^2\mathclose{\text{.}}πr2. It uses the derivatives of the sine and cosine (Module 5). They rest on the limit sin⁡θ/θ→1,\sin\theta/\theta \to 1\mathclose{\text{,}}sinθ/θ→1, and Module 2 proved that limit with the area π\piπ of the disc of radius 1, taken from geometry. What the example proves is that this one fact gives the area of every disc and of every ellipse.

Back to x with a triangle

In an indefinite integral the answer comes out in terms of θ\thetaθ and must be written in terms of xxx again. A right triangle does it. Draw one with an angle θ\thetaθ whose sides make the substitution true; Pythagoras’ theorem gives the third side, and the other trigonometric functions of θ\thetaθ can be read off (Figure 11.2).

Partial fractions

Adding fractions is school algebra:

2x−2+3x+1=2(x+1)+3(x−2)(x−2)(x+1)=5x−4x2−x−2.\begin{aligned} \frac{2}{x - 2} + \frac{3}{x + 1} &= \frac{2(x + 1) + 3(x - 2)}{(x - 2)(x + 1)} \\ &= \frac{5x - 4}{x^2 - x - 2}. \end{aligned}x−22​+x+13​​=(x−2)(x+1)2(x+1)+3(x−2)​=x2−x−25x−4​.​

The left side is easy to integrate, to 2ln⁡∣x−2∣+3ln⁡∣x+1∣+C.2\ln\abs{x - 2} + 3\ln\abs{x + 1} + C\mathclose{\text{.}}2ln∣x−2∣+3ln∣x+1∣+C. So the right side is easy to integrate too, once you can run the addition backwards. Writing a rational function as a sum of simpler fractions of this kind is called decomposing it into partial fractions. Every rational function can be decomposed, with a polynomial added in front when it is improper (below).

Definition 11.1Proper and improper rational functions

A rational function P(x)Q(x)\dfrac{P(x)}{Q(x)}Q(x)P(x)​ (Module 1) is proper if the degree of the polynomial PPP is less than the degree of Q,Q\mathclose{\text{,}}Q, and improper otherwise.

Long division of polynomials turns an improper rational function into a polynomial plus a proper one: dividing PPP by QQQ gives a quotient SSS and a remainder R,R\mathclose{\text{,}}R, polynomials with P=SQ+RP = SQ + RP=SQ+R and deg⁡R<deg⁡Q,\deg R < \deg Q\mathclose{\text{,}}degR<degQ, so that

P(x)Q(x)=S(x)+R(x)Q(x).\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} = S(x) + \frac{R(x)}{Q(x)}.Q(x)P(x)​=S(x)+Q(x)R(x)​.

The polynomial SSS is integrated term by term; partial fractions are for the proper part.

Distinct linear factors

Start with a denominator that is a product of different linear factors, such as x2−x−2=(x−2)(x+1),x^2 - x - 2 = (x - 2)(x + 1)\mathclose{\text{,}}x2−x−2=(x−2)(x+1), and suppose you did not know the answer above. Look for constants AAA and BBB with

Put x=2:x = 2\mathclose{\text{:}}x=2: 6=3A,6 = 3A\mathclose{\text{,}}6=3A, so A=2.A = 2\mathclose{\text{.}}A=2. Put x=−1:x = -1\mathclose{\text{:}}x=−1: −9=−3B,-9 = -3B\mathclose{\text{,}}−9=−3B, so B=3.B = 3\mathclose{\text{.}}B=3. To find A,A\mathclose{\text{,}}A, the coefficient of 1x−2,\dfrac{1}{x - 2}\mathclose{\text{,}}x−21​, cover up the factor x−2x - 2x−2 in the denominator of the left side and put x=2x = 2x=2 in what is left: 5⋅2−42+1=2.\dfrac{5\cdot 2 - 4}{2 + 1} = 2\mathclose{\text{.}}2+15⋅2−4​=2. for xxx near 2; as x→2,x \to 2\mathclose{\text{,}}x→2, the left side tends to its value at 2 and the last term tends to 0, which leaves A.A\mathclose{\text{.}}A.

Key idea

The cover-up method. If x−rx - rx−r is a factor of the denominator Q(x)Q(x)Q(x) that appears only once, the coefficient of 1x−r\dfrac{1}{x - r}x−r1​ in the decomposition of P(x)Q(x)\dfrac{P(x)}{Q(x)}Q(x)P(x)​ is the value at x=rx = rx=r of the fraction with the factor x−rx - rx−r covered up.

Repeated and quadratic factors

Two things can complicate a denominator. A factor may be repeated, as in (x−1)2(x+1).(x - 1)^2(x + 1)\mathclose{\text{.}}(x−1)2(x+1). And a quadratic factor such as x2+1x^2 + 1x2+1 may have no real zeros, so that it does not split into real linear factors. A quadratic x2+px+qx^2 + px + qx2+px+q with p2<4qp^2 < 4qp2<4q (a negative discriminant) is called irreducible. A theorem of algebra, which this series uses without proof, says that every polynomial with real coefficients is a product of a constant, linear factors and irreducible quadratic factors. (It follows from the fundamental theorem of algebra.) So the next theorem covers every proper rational function, at least in principle: finding the factors of QQQ can be the hard part.

Theorem 11.7Partial fraction decomposition

Let P(x)Q(x)\dfrac{P(x)}{Q(x)}Q(x)P(x)​ be a proper rational function, and let QQQ be factored as a constant times powers of different linear factors x−rx - rx−r and of different irreducible quadratic factors x2+px+q.x^2 + px + q\mathclose{\text{.}}x2+px+q. Then P(x)Q(x)\dfrac{P(x)}{Q(x)}Q(x)P(x)​ is a sum of the following terms, with unique constants:

  • for each factor (x−r)k(x - r)^k(x−r)k of Q,Q\mathclose{\text{,}}Q, the kkk terms A1x−r+A2(x−r)2+⋯+Ak(x−r)k;\dfrac{A_1}{x - r} + \dfrac{A_2}{(x - r)^2} + \dots + \dfrac{A_k}{(x - r)^k}\mathclose{\text{;}}x−rA1​​+(x−r)2A2​​+⋯+(x−r)kAk​​;
  • for each factor (x2+px+q)m\big(x^2 + px + q\big)^m(x2+px+q)m of Q,Q\mathclose{\text{,}}Q, the mmm terms B1x+C1x2+px+q+⋯+Bmx+Cm(x2+px+q)m.\dfrac{B_1x + C_1}{x^2 + px + q} + \dots + \dfrac{B_mx + C_m}{\big(x^2 + px + q\big)^m}\mathclose{\text{.}}x2+px+qB1​x+C1​​+⋯+(x2+px+q)mBm​x+Cm​​.

Theorem 11.6 is the case in which every power is 1 and there are no quadratic factors; the general case is proved in algebra courses, and this series uses it without proof. To find the constants, multiply by Q(x)Q(x)Q(x) and compare coefficients, or put convenient values of x;x\mathclose{\text{;}}x; the cover-up method still gives the coefficient of the highest power of each linear factor. Each term then integrates with the methods you know: a power of x−rx - rx−r by the power rule or to a logarithm, and a quadratic term by completing the square, a logarithm and an arctangent. (A power m≥2m \ge 2m≥2 of an irreducible quadratic needs a trigonometric substitution as well.)

Comparing the coefficients of x2x^2x2 gives 2=1+B,2 = 1 + B\mathclose{\text{,}}2=1+B, so B=1,B = 1\mathclose{\text{,}}B=1, and the constant terms give 4=1+D,4 = 1 + D\mathclose{\text{,}}4=1+D, so D=3;D = 3\mathclose{\text{;}}D=3; the coefficients of xxx agree, 4=B+D.4 = B + D\mathclose{\text{.}}4=B+D. So the integrand is

1x+1+xx2+1+3x2+1,\frac{1}{x + 1} + \frac{x}{x^2 + 1} + \frac{3}{x^2 + 1},x+11​+x2+1x​+x2+13​,

and, with the substitution w=x2+1w = x^2 + 1w=x2+1 for the middle term,

∫2x2+4x+4(x+1)(x2+1) dx=ln⁡∣x+1∣+12ln⁡(x2+1)+3arctan⁡x+C.\begin{aligned} &\int \frac{2x^2 + 4x + 4}{(x + 1)\big(x^2 + 1\big)}\,dx \\ &\quad= \ln\abs{x + 1} + \tfrac12\ln\big(x^2 + 1\big) \\ &\qquad + 3\arctan x + C. \end{aligned}​∫(x+1)(x2+1)2x2+4x+4​dx=ln∣x+1∣+21​ln(x2+1)+3arctanx+C.​
Watch out

Four slips with partial fractions. (1) Not dividing first. x3x2−1\dfrac{x^3}{x^2 - 1}x2−1x3​ is improper; it is x+xx2−1,x + \dfrac{x}{x^2 - 1}\mathclose{\text{,}}x+x2−1x​, and only the second part has the form Ax−1+Bx+1.\dfrac{A}{x - 1} + \dfrac{B}{x + 1}\mathclose{\text{.}}x−1A​+x+1B​. (2) Leaving out a power of a repeated factor. In Example 11.17(a), the form B(x−1)2+Dx+1\dfrac{B}{(x - 1)^2} + \dfrac{D}{x + 1}(x−1)2B​+x+1D​ without Ax−1\dfrac{A}{x - 1}x−1A​ has no solution: in 4x=B(x+1)+D(x−1)2,4x = B(x + 1) + D(x - 1)^2\mathclose{\text{,}}4x=B(x+1)+D(x−1)2, the terms in x2x^2x2 give D=0,D = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}D=0, then the terms in xxx give B=4,B = 4\mathclose{\text{,}}B=4, and then the constant terms say 0=B+D=4.0 = B + D = 4\mathclose{\text{.}}0=B+D=4. (3) A constant numerator over an irreducible quadratic: it must be Bx+C.Bx + C\mathclose{\text{.}}Bx+C. (4) Missing a substitution: ∫x2+1x3+3x dx=13ln⁡∣x3+3x∣+C\displaystyle\int \frac{x^2 + 1}{x^3 + 3x}\,dx = \tfrac13\ln\abs{x^3 + 3x} + C∫x3+3xx2+1​dx=31​ln​x3+3x​+C with u=x3+3x,u = x^3 + 3x\mathclose{\text{,}}u=x3+3x, no partial fractions needed.

Compute itPartial fractions with SymPy

SymPy’s factor finds the factors, div divides polynomials, and apart decomposes a rational function into partial fractions:

Python
import sympy as sp
x = sp.symbols('x')
P = x**3 + 2*x**2 + 2*x - 2
Q = x**2 + x - 2
print(sp.factor(Q))
print(sp.div(P, Q, x))                  # (quotient, remainder)
print(sp.apart(P/Q, x))                 # Example 11.16
print(sp.apart((2*x**2 + 4*x + 4)/((x + 1)*(x**2 + 1)), x))
Output
(x - 1)*(x + 2)
(x + 1, 3*x)
x + 1 + 2/(x + 2) + 1/(x - 1)
(x + 3)/(x**2 + 1) + 1/(x + 1)

These are Example 11.16, in SymPy’s order of terms, and Example 11.17(b) before its last split. SymPy factors over the rational numbers, so a denominator such as x2−2,x^2 - 2\mathclose{\text{,}}x2−2, whose zeros ±2\pm\sqrt2±2​ are irrational, stays whole unless you say which numbers to allow:

Python
print(sp.apart(1/(x**2 - 2), x))
print(sp.apart(1/(x**2 - 2), x, extension=sp.sqrt(2)))
Output
1/(x**2 - 2)
-sqrt(2)/(4*(x + sqrt(2))) + sqrt(2)/(4*(x - sqrt(2)))

The second answer is Example 11.15(b) with a=2,a = \sqrt2\mathclose{\text{,}}a=2​, since 122=24.\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt2} = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{4}\mathclose{\text{.}}22​1​=42​​.

5

A strategy for integration

Differentiation is mechanical: the rules of Modules 4 to 6 differentiate every formula built from the catalogue of Module 1. Integration is not. No set of rules always works, the same integrand may give way to several methods, and some integrands give way to none (Section 11.6). What you have is a toolbox and a checklist.

Key idea

A strategy for integration.

  1. Simplify the integrand if you can: expand, cancel, split a fraction, use an identity such as sin⁡xcos⁡x=12sin⁡2x\sin x\cos x = \tfrac12\sin 2xsinxcosx=21​sin2x or tan⁡2x=sec⁡2x−1.\tan^2 x = \sec^2 x - 1\mathclose{\text{.}}tan2x=sec2x−1. Then look in the table of Section 10.1.
  2. Substitute if the integrand contains a function together with its derivative, perhaps up to a constant factor (Section 10.7).
  3. Classify the integrand by its form:
    • a product of a power of xxx with ekx,e^{kx}\mathclose{\text{,}}ekx, sin⁡kx\sin kxsinkx or cos⁡kx,\cos kx\mathclose{\text{,}}coskx, or with ln⁡x\ln xlnx or an inverse trigonometric function: by parts (Section 11.1);
    • powers of trigonometric functions: identities and substitutions (Section 11.2);
    • a2−x2,\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}\mathclose{\text{,}}a2−x2​, a2+x2\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}a2+x2​ or x2−a2,\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}\mathclose{\text{,}}x2−a2​, perhaps after completing the square: a trigonometric substitution (Section 11.3);
    • a rational function: long division if it is improper, then partial fractions (Section 11.4);
    • a root g(x)n:\sqrt[n]{g(x)}\mathclose{\text{:}}ng(x)​: try u=g(x)n.u = \sqrt[n]{g(x)}\mathclose{\text{.}}u=ng(x)​.
  4. Try again: combine methods (a substitution, then parts), multiply by a clever form of 1 (as for sec⁡x),\sec x\mathclose{\text{),}}secx), or relate the integral to one you have done. If nothing works, the integrand may have no elementary antiderivative (Section 11.6): compute the integral numerically (Section 11.7).
Example 11.18Choosing a method✓ Checked

Choose a method for each integral, and evaluate it.

  • (a) ∫xx2+4 dx\displaystyle\int \frac{x}{x^2 + 4}\,dx∫x2+4x​dx
  • (b) ∫ex dx,\displaystyle\int e^{\sqrt x}\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}∫ex​dx, for x>0x > 0x>0
  • (c) ∫dxx2−4x+13\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{x^2 - 4x + 13}∫x2−4x+13dx​
  • (d) ∫x1+x dx,\displaystyle\int \frac{\sqrt x}{1 + x}\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}∫1+xx​​dx, for x>0x > 0x>0

(a) A rational function, but step 2 comes first: the numerator is half the derivative of the denominator. With u=x2+4,u = x^2 + 4\mathclose{\text{,}}u=x2+4, du=2x dx:du = 2x\,dx\mathclose{\text{:}}du=2xdx:

∫xx2+4 dx=12∫duu=12ln⁡(x2+4)+C.\begin{aligned} \int \frac{x}{x^2 + 4}\,dx &= \frac12\int \frac{du}{u} \\ &= \frac12\ln\big(x^2 + 4\big) + C. \end{aligned}∫x2+4x​dx​=21​∫udu​=21​ln(x2+4)+C.​

(b) A root: let w=x,w = \sqrt x\mathclose{\text{,}}w=x​, so that x=w2x = w^2x=w2 and dx=2w dwdx = 2w\,dwdx=2wdw (Theorem 11.5(b), with the one-to-one substitution x=w2,x = w^2\mathclose{\text{,}}x=w2, w>0).w > 0\mathclose{\text{).}}w>0). The integral becomes 2∫wew dw,2\int we^w\,dw\mathclose{\text{,}}2∫wewdw, a product for parts: with u=wu = wu=w and dv=ew dw,dv = e^w\,dw\mathclose{\text{,}}dv=ewdw,

2∫wew dw=2(wew−ew)+C=2(x−1)ex+C.\begin{aligned} 2\int we^w\,dw &= 2\big(we^w - e^w\big) + C \\ &= 2\big(\sqrt x - 1\big)e^{\sqrt x} + C. \end{aligned}2∫wewdw​=2(wew−ew)+C=2(x​−1)ex​+C.​

(c) A rational function whose denominator has no real zeros, since (−4)2−4⋅13=−36<0.(-4)^2 - 4\cdot 13 = -36 < 0\mathclose{\text{.}}(−4)2−4⋅13=−36<0. Complete the square, x2−4x+13=(x−2)2+9,x^2 - 4x + 13 = (x - 2)^2 + 9\mathclose{\text{,}}x2−4x+13=(x−2)2+9, and use ∫duu2+a2=1aarctan⁡ua+C\int \frac{du}{u^2 + a^2} = \frac1a\arctan\frac{u}{a} + C∫u2+a2du​=a1​arctanau​+C (Example 10.11) with u=x−2u = x - 2u=x−2 and a=3:a = 3\mathclose{\text{:}}a=3:

∫dxx2−4x+13=13arctan⁡x−23+C.\begin{aligned} &\int \frac{dx}{x^2 - 4x + 13} \\ &\quad= \frac13\arctan\frac{x - 2}{3} + C. \end{aligned}​∫x2−4x+13dx​=31​arctan3x−2​+C.​

(d) A root again: w=x,w = \sqrt x\mathclose{\text{,}}w=x​, dx=2w dw,dx = 2w\,dw\mathclose{\text{,}}dx=2wdw, gives 2∫w21+w2 dw,2\int \dfrac{w^2}{1 + w^2}\,dw\mathclose{\text{,}}2∫1+w2w2​dw, an improper rational function. Divide, or write w2=(1+w2)−1:w^2 = (1 + w^2) - 1\mathclose{\text{:}}w2=(1+w2)−1:

2∫w21+w2 dw=2∫(1−11+w2) dw=2w−2arctan⁡w+C=2x−2arctan⁡x+C.\begin{aligned} &2\int \frac{w^2}{1 + w^2}\,dw \\ &\quad= 2\int \Big(1 - \frac{1}{1 + w^2}\Big)\,dw \\ &\quad= 2w - 2\arctan w + C \\ &\quad= 2\sqrt x - 2\arctan\sqrt x + C. \end{aligned}​2∫1+w2w2​dw=2∫(1−1+w21​)dw=2w−2arctanw+C=2x​−2arctanx​+C.​
Watch out

Reaching for a heavy method when a light one works. ∫xx2+4 dx\int \dfrac{x}{x^2 + 4}\,dx∫x2+4x​dx needs no partial fractions, and ∫xx2+1 dx\int x\sqrt{x^2 + 1}\,dx∫xx2+1​dx needs no trigonometric substitution: u=x2+1u = x^2 + 1u=x2+1 gives 13(x2+1)3/2+C\tfrac13\big(x^2 + 1\big)^{3/2} + C31​(x2+1)3/2+C in one line. Look for a substitution before anything else.

6

Integration by computer

Computer algebra systems such as SymPy integrate with the methods of this module and with algorithms that handle whole families of integrands at once. Module 10 introduced sp.integrate (Section 10.8); here it is on integrals of this module, with the lesson of Module 10 in mind: an answer that looks different is not necessarily wrong.

Compute itIntegrals of this module by computer
Python
import sympy as sp
x = sp.symbols('x')
print(sp.integrate(x**2*sp.sin(x), x))                 # Example 11.3
print(sp.integrate(sp.exp(x)*sp.sin(x), x))            # Example 11.6
print(sp.integrate((5*x - 4)/(x**2 - x - 2), x))       # Example 11.15(a)
print(sp.integrate(1/sp.sqrt(x**2 + 4), x))            # Example 11.14(a)
print(sp.integrate(sp.sec(x), x))                      # Theorem 11.4
Output
-x**2*cos(x) + 2*x*sin(x) + 2*cos(x)
exp(x)*sin(x)/2 - exp(x)*cos(x)/2
2*log(x - 2) + 3*log(x + 1)
asinh(x/2)
-log(sin(x) - 1)/2 + log(sin(x) + 1)/2

The first two are the answers of Examples 11.3 and 11.6, in SymPy’s order of terms. The third writes ln⁡(x−2)\ln(x - 2)ln(x−2) for ln⁡∣x−2∣,\ln\abs{x - 2}\mathclose{\text{,}}ln∣x−2∣, as Module 10 explained: SymPy’s log works with complex numbers, and its answer is right where x>2.x > 2\mathclose{\text{.}}x>2. The fourth is arsinh⁡x2=ln⁡(x2+x24+1)=ln⁡(x+x2+4)−ln⁡2,\operatorname{arsinh}\dfrac{x}{2} = \ln\Big(\dfrac{x}{2} + \sqrt{\dfrac{x^2}{4} + 1}\Big) = \ln\big(x + \sqrt{x^2 + 4}\big) - \ln 2\mathclose{\text{,}}arsinh2x​=ln(2x​+4x2​+1​)=ln(x+x2+4​)−ln2, by Exercise 6.10: Example 11.14’s answer minus the constant ln⁡2.\ln 2\mathclose{\text{.}}ln2. The fifth looks nothing like ln⁡∣sec⁡x+tan⁡x∣.\ln\abs{\sec x + \tan x}\mathclose{\text{.}}ln∣secx+tanx∣. Where cos⁡x≠0,\cos x \ne 0\mathclose{\text{,}}cosx=0, sin⁡x−1<0,\sin x - 1 < 0\mathclose{\text{,}}sinx−1<0, so SymPy’s ln⁡(sin⁡x−1)\ln(\sin x - 1)ln(sinx−1) is a complex number, ln⁡(1−sin⁡x)\ln(1 - \sin x)ln(1−sinx) plus the constant πi.\pi i\mathclose{\text{.}}πi. Up to a constant, then, SymPy’s answer is

12ln⁡1+sin⁡x1−sin⁡x=12ln⁡(1+sin⁡x)2cos⁡2x=ln⁡∣sec⁡x+tan⁡x∣,\begin{aligned} \frac12\ln\frac{1 + \sin x}{1 - \sin x} &= \frac12\ln\frac{(1 + \sin x)^2}{\cos^2 x} \\ &= \ln\abs{\sec x + \tan x}, \end{aligned}21​ln1−sinx1+sinx​​=21​lncos2x(1+sinx)2​=ln∣secx+tanx∣,​

where the middle step multiplies the top and the bottom by 1+sin⁡x.1 + \sin x\mathclose{\text{.}}1+sinx. Two right answers, again. To check an answer, differentiate it:

Python
mine = sp.log(x + sp.sqrt(x**2 + 4))                   # Example 11.14(a)
print(sp.simplify(sp.diff(mine, x) - 1/sp.sqrt(x**2 + 4)))
print(sp.simplify(sp.diff(sp.log(sp.sec(x) + sp.tan(x)), x) - sp.sec(x)))
print(sp.N((mine - sp.asinh(x/2)).subs(x, 3)), sp.N(sp.log(2)))
Output
0
0
0.693147180559945 0.693147180559945

Both differences of derivatives are 0, and the difference between Example 11.14’s answer and SymPy’s, at x=3x = 3x=3 or anywhere else, is ln⁡2.\ln 2\mathclose{\text{.}}ln2. Finally, an integral that defeats SymPy, the length of an arch of the sine curve in Module 12:

Python
print(sp.integrate(sp.sqrt(1 + sp.cos(x)**2), x))
Output
Integral(sqrt(cos(x)**2 + 1), x)

SymPy returns the integral unevaluated: it has found no antiderivative.

Watch out

Three things to remember about a computer’s antiderivative. (1) It leaves out “+ C+\,C+C” and usually the absolute value bars, and it may use complex logarithms. (2) A different-looking answer may well be right: differentiate it, or compare it with yours at a few points of one interval, where the difference must be the same constant. (3) An unevaluated Integral(...) means that SymPy found no antiderivative, not that none exists; and a correct answer can be so long that a numerical value (Section 11.7) is more useful.

Functions with no elementary antiderivative

The integral of the last Compute it box is not unusual. Most of the functions in this module’s examples were chosen because their antiderivatives can be written down; many functions that turn up in practice cannot be integrated that way.

Definition 11.2Elementary function

An elementary function is a function that can be built from constants and xxx with finitely many additions, subtractions, multiplications, divisions, powers, roots, exponentials, logarithms, trigonometric and inverse trigonometric functions, and compositions of these.

Every function of Module 1’s catalogue is elementary, and so are combinations such as e−x2,e^{-x^2}\mathclose{\text{,}}e−x2, 1+cos⁡2x,\sqrt{1 + \cos^2 x}\mathclose{\text{,}}1+cos2x​, sinh⁡x=12(ex−e−x)\sinh x = \tfrac12\big(e^x - e^{-x}\big)sinhx=21​(ex−e−x) and ln⁡(x+x2+1).\ln\big(x + \sqrt{x^2 + 1}\big)\mathclose{\text{.}}ln(x+x2+1​). The derivative of an elementary function is elementary: the rules of Modules 4 to 6 produce it. The antiderivative of an elementary function need not be. Liouville’s theorem describes what an elementary antiderivative must look like, if there is one; from it one can prove that none of

e−x2,sin⁡xx,1ln⁡x,exx,sin⁡(x2)e^{-x^2}, \quad \frac{\sin x}{x}, \quad \frac{1}{\ln x}, \quad \frac{e^x}{x}, \quad \sin\big(x^2\big)e−x2,xsinx​,lnx1​,xex​,sin(x2)

has an elementary antiderivative; nor has ex2,e^{x^2}\mathclose{\text{,}}ex2, which Example 11.2 met. This series proves neither Liouville’s theorem nor these consequences of it: the proofs need algebra beyond the series. What they mean is not beyond it: no cleverness with the methods of this module will find such an antiderivative, because none exists.

These functions do have antiderivatives, all the same. Each is continuous on every interval inside its domain, so by Part 1 of the Fundamental Theorem (Section 10.4) an area function ∫axf(t) dt,\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\mathclose{\text{,}}∫ax​f(t)dt, with aaa in such an interval, is an antiderivative there. The most useful of them have names, and their values are computed numerically, in the same way as calculators compute sin⁡x\sin xsinx and ln⁡x.\ln x\mathclose{\text{.}}lnx.

Definition 11.3Three functions defined by integrals
  • The error function is erf⁡x=2π∫0xe−t2 dt,\operatorname{erf} x = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\displaystyle\int_0^x e^{-t^2}\,dt\mathclose{\text{,}}erfx=π​2​∫0x​e−t2dt, for every real xxx (Module 10).
  • The sine integral is Si⁡x=∫0xsin⁡tt dt,\operatorname{Si} x = \displaystyle\int_0^x \frac{\sin t}{t}\,dt\mathclose{\text{,}}Six=∫0x​tsint​dt, for every real x,x\mathclose{\text{,}}x, where the integrand is given the value 1 at t=0,t = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}t=0, its limit there (Module 2), so that it is continuous.
  • The logarithmic integral is Li⁡x=∫2xdtln⁡t,\operatorname{Li} x = \displaystyle\int_2^x \frac{dt}{\ln t}\mathclose{\text{,}}Lix=∫2x​lntdt​, for x>1.x > 1\mathclose{\text{.}}x>1.

By Part 1 of the Fundamental Theorem, (erf⁡x)′=2πe−x2,(\operatorname{erf} x)' = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt\pi}e^{-x^2}\mathclose{\text{,}}(erfx)′=π​2​e−x2, (Si⁡x)′=sin⁡xx(\operatorname{Si} x)' = \dfrac{\sin x}{x}(Six)′=xsinx​ for x≠0,x \ne 0\mathclose{\text{,}}x=0, and (Li⁡x)′=1ln⁡x.(\operatorname{Li} x)' = \dfrac{1}{\ln x}\mathclose{\text{.}}(Lix)′=lnx1​. Figure 11.3 shows the three, and here are a few values of the first two:

xxxerf⁡x\operatorname{erf} xerfxSi⁡x\operatorname{Si} xSix

The error function is the workhorse of probability, where e−x2e^{-x^2}e−x2 is the shape of the normal distribution (Module 12). The sine integral turns up in signal processing and optics. The logarithmic integral counts primes: the number of prime numbers up to xxx is close to Li⁡x\operatorname{Li} xLix when xxx is large, in the sense that their ratio tends to 1 as x→∞.x \to \infty\mathclose{\text{.}}x→∞. That is the prime number theorem, and the Compute it box below compares the two at a million.

Compute itSpecial functions in SymPy

Asked for these antiderivatives, SymPy names them:

Python
import sympy as sp
x = sp.symbols('x')
for f in [sp.exp(-x**2), sp.sin(x)/x, 1/sp.log(x), sp.exp(x)/x]:
    print(sp.integrate(f, x))
Output
sqrt(pi)*erf(x)/2
Si(x)
li(x)
Ei(x)

Ei is the exponential integral, another named antiderivative. SymPy’s li is another antiderivative of 1ln⁡x,\dfrac{1}{\ln x}\mathclose{\text{,}}lnx1​, defined by an integral from 0 that needs special care at t=1,t = 1\mathclose{\text{,}}t=1, where 1ln⁡t\dfrac{1}{\ln t}lnt1​ is undefined; it differs from Li⁡\operatorname{Li}Li by the constant li⁡2.\operatorname{li} 2\mathclose{\text{.}}li2. The prime numbers up to a million, counted by primepi, against Li⁡\operatorname{Li}Li of a million:

Python
print(sp.N(sp.li(2)))
print(sp.primepi(10**6), sp.N(sp.Li(10**6)))
print(sp.Integral(sp.exp(-x**2), (x, 0, 1)).evalf())
Output
1.04516378011749
78498 78626.5039956821
0.746824132812427

There are 78,498 primes below a million, and Li⁡106≈78,627:\operatorname{Li} 10^6 \approx 78{,}627\mathclose{\text{:}}Li106≈78,627: a difference of less than 0.2%. The last line is ∫01e−x2 dx,\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}∫01​e−x2dx, which evalf computes numerically, the value that Module 9 estimated with midpoint sums.

Watch out

“No elementary antiderivative” does not mean “no antiderivative”, and it does not stop you from evaluating definite integrals: ∫01e−x2 dx≈0.746824\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx \approx 0.746824∫01​e−x2dx≈0.746824 is a perfectly good number. And small changes matter. ∫xe−x2 dx=−12e−x2+C\int xe^{-x^2}\,dx = -\tfrac12e^{-x^2} + C∫xe−x2dx=−21​e−x2+C and ∫xsin⁡(x2) dx=−12cos⁡(x2)+C,\int x\sin\big(x^2\big)\,dx = -\tfrac12\cos\big(x^2\big) + C\mathclose{\text{,}}∫xsin(x2)dx=−21​cos(x2)+C, by substitution; without the factor x,x\mathclose{\text{,}}x, neither has an elementary antiderivative.

7

Numerical integration

Two kinds of integral call for numbers rather than formulas: integrals of functions with no elementary antiderivative, such as ∫01e−x2 dx,\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx\mathclose{\text{,}}∫01​e−x2dx, and integrals of functions known only through measurements, such as a speed or a power read every few seconds. A numerical integration rule computes an integral from values of the integrand. The midpoint sum of Module 9 is one, the midpoint rule

Mn=Δx [f(xˉ1)+f(xˉ2)+⋯+f(xˉn)],M_n = \Delta x\,\big[f(\bar x_1) + f(\bar x_2) + \dots + f(\bar x_n)\big],Mn​=Δx[f(xˉ1​)+f(xˉ2​)+⋯+f(xˉn​)],

where Δx=b−an,\Delta x = \tfrac{b - a}{n}\mathclose{\text{,}}Δx=nb−a​, xi=a+i Δx,x_i = a + i\,\Delta x\mathclose{\text{,}}xi​=a+iΔx, and xˉi=12(xi−1+xi)\bar x_i = \tfrac12(x_{i-1} + x_i)xˉi​=21​(xi−1​+xi​) is the midpoint of the iiith subinterval (read “x bar i”; Module 9 wrote mi).m_i\mathclose{\text{).}}mi​). Its error shrank like 1n2\tfrac{1}{n^2}n21​ (Section 9.3). This section adds two rules, explains why the errors behave as they do, and bounds them.

The trapezoidal rule

In Example 9.2 a car’s speed was read every 2 seconds. The left and right sums gave 100 m and 140 m, and their average, 120 m, was a better single estimate. Averaging LnL_nLn​ and RnR_nRn​ term by term gives

Ln+Rn2=∑i=1nf(xi−1)+f(xi)2 Δx,\frac{L_n + R_n}{2} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{f(x_{i-1}) + f(x_i)}{2}\,\Delta x,2Ln​+Rn​​=i=1∑n​2f(xi−1​)+f(xi​)​Δx,

and each term is the area of a trapezoid: when fff is positive, the region under the chord that joins the points (xi−1,f(xi−1))(x_{i-1}, f(x_{i-1}))(xi−1​,f(xi−1​)) and (xi,f(xi))(x_i, f(x_i))(xi​,f(xi​)) of the graph (Figure 11.4, left). Every value of fff except the first and the last belongs to two neighbouring trapezoids, so collecting terms gives the following rule.

Definition 11.4The trapezoidal rule

Let fff be defined on [a,b],[a, b]\mathclose{\text{,}}[a,b], let n≥1n \ge 1n≥1 be a whole number, Δx=b−an\Delta x = \tfrac{b - a}{n}Δx=nb−a​ and xi=a+i Δx.x_i = a + i\,\Delta x\mathclose{\text{.}}xi​=a+iΔx. The trapezoidal rule with nnn subintervals is

Tn=Δx2[f(x0)+2f(x1)+2f(x2)+…+2f(xn−1)+f(xn)].\begin{aligned} T_n = \frac{\Delta x}{2}\big[&f(x_0) + 2f(x_1) \\ &+ 2f(x_2) + \dots \\ &+ 2f(x_{n-1}) + f(x_n)\big]. \end{aligned}Tn​=2Δx​[​f(x0​)+2f(x1​)+2f(x2​)+…+2f(xn−1​)+f(xn​)].​

It is the average 12(Ln+Rn)\tfrac12(L_n + R_n)21​(Ln​+Rn​) of the left and right sums.

The error of a rule is the integral minus the approximation: ET=∫abf(x) dx−TnE_T = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx - T_nET​=∫ab​f(x)dx−Tn​ and EM=∫abf(x) dx−Mn.E_M = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx - M_n\mathclose{\text{.}}EM​=∫ab​f(x)dx−Mn​. A positive error means that the rule underestimates.

Two patterns stand out. Each time nnn doubles, both errors are divided by about 4, as Module 9 found for midpoint sums. And at every n,n\mathclose{\text{,}}n, ET≈−2EM.E_T \approx -2E_M\mathclose{\text{.}}ET​≈−2EM​.

The signs come from the shape of the graph. The second derivative of 1x\tfrac1xx1​ is 2x3,\tfrac{2}{x^3}\mathclose{\text{,}}x32​, positive for every x>0,x > 0\mathclose{\text{,}}x>0, so the graph is concave up on (0,∞),(0, \infty)\mathclose{\text{,}}(0,∞), an open interval that contains [1,2][1, 2][1,2] (Section 8.4). It sags below each chord, and each trapezoid covers more than the region under the graph. So TnT_nTn​ overestimates (Figure 11.4, left). For the midpoint rule, draw the tangent line at the midpoint of a subinterval. It passes through the middle of the top of the midpoint rectangle and cuts off two triangles of equal area, one above the top on one side and one below it on the other. So the rectangle has the same area as the trapezoid under the tangent line (Figure 11.4, right). A concave-up graph lies above its tangent lines (Theorem 8.11), so that trapezoid lies below the graph, and MnM_nMn​ underestimates. For a graph that is concave down, both conclusions turn round, as Module 9 saw in Exercise 9.2, where M4M_4M4​ overestimated ∫02(4−x2) dx.\int_0^2 (4 - x^2)\,dx\mathclose{\text{.}}∫02​(4−x2)dx.

Simpson’s rule

The trapezoidal rule replaces the graph by chords, straight lines through two points. A parabola through three points can follow a curve much more closely, and the area under one is easy to find. Let y=Ax2+Bx+Cy = Ax^2 + Bx + Cy=Ax2+Bx+C pass through the points (−h,y0),(-h, y_0)\mathclose{\text{,}}(−h,y0​), (0,y1)(0, y_1)(0,y1​) and (h,y2),(h, y_2)\mathclose{\text{,}}(h,y2​), where h>0.h > 0\mathclose{\text{.}}h>0. Then, since the odd term BxBxBx contributes 0,

∫−hh(Ax2+Bx+C) dx=23Ah3+2Ch=h3(2Ah2+6C).\begin{aligned} \int_{-h}^{h} \big(Ax^2 + Bx + C\big)\,dx &= \frac23Ah^3 + 2Ch \\ &= \frac{h}{3}\big(2Ah^2 + 6C\big). \end{aligned}∫−hh​(Ax2+Bx+C)dx​=32​Ah3+2Ch=3h​(2Ah2+6C).​

The three points give y0=Ah2−Bh+C,y_0 = Ah^2 - Bh + C\mathclose{\text{,}}y0​=Ah2−Bh+C, y1=Cy_1 = Cy1​=C and y2=Ah2+Bh+C,y_2 = Ah^2 + Bh + C\mathclose{\text{,}}y2​=Ah2+Bh+C, so y0+4y1+y2=2Ah2+6C,y_0 + 4y_1 + y_2 = 2Ah^2 + 6C\mathclose{\text{,}}y0​+4y1​+y2​=2Ah2+6C, and the area is

h3(y0+4y1+y2).\frac{h}{3}\big(y_0 + 4y_1 + y_2\big).3h​(y0​+4y1​+y2​).

Such a parabola always exists: C=y1,C = y_1\mathclose{\text{,}}C=y1​, B=y2−y02hB = \tfrac{y_2 - y_0}{2h}B=2hy2​−y0​​ and A=y0−2y1+y22h2A = \tfrac{y_0 - 2y_1 + y_2}{2h^2}A=2h2y0​−2y1​+y2​​ (a straight line if A=0).A = 0\mathclose{\text{).}}A=0). The area depends only on the three heights and the spacing h,h\mathclose{\text{,}}h, so it is the same for any three equally spaced points, wherever they are on the xxx-axis: sliding the picture sideways does not change it. Now cut [a,b][a, b][a,b] into an even number nnn of subintervals, pass a parabola through the points of the graph above x0,x_0\mathclose{\text{,}}x0​, x1x_1x1​ and x2,x_2\mathclose{\text{,}}x2​, another through those above x2,x_2\mathclose{\text{,}}x2​, x3x_3x3​ and x4,x_4\mathclose{\text{,}}x4​, and so on, and add up the areas under them (Figure 11.5, left).

Definition 11.5Simpson’s rule

Let nnn be even, Δx=b−an\Delta x = \tfrac{b - a}{n}Δx=nb−a​ and xi=a+i Δx.x_i = a + i\,\Delta x\mathclose{\text{.}}xi​=a+iΔx. Simpson’s rule with nnn subintervals is

Sn=Δx3[f(x0)+4f(x1)+2f(x2)+4f(x3)+⋯+2f(xn−2)+4f(xn−1)+f(xn)].\begin{aligned} S_n = \frac{\Delta x}{3}\big[&f(x_0) + 4f(x_1) + 2f(x_2) \\ &+ 4f(x_3) + \dots + 2f(x_{n-2}) \\ &+ 4f(x_{n-1}) + f(x_n)\big]. \end{aligned}Sn​=3Δx​[​f(x0​)+4f(x1​)+2f(x2​)+4f(x3​)+⋯+2f(xn−2​)+4f(xn−1​)+f(xn​)].​

The coefficients follow the pattern 1,4,2,4,2,…,4,1:1, 4, 2, 4, 2, \dots, 4, 1\mathclose{\text{:}}1,4,2,4,2,…,4,1: each point with an odd index is the middle of a pair of subintervals, with weight 4, and each interior point with an even index is shared by two pairs, with weight 1+1=2.1 + 1 = 2\mathclose{\text{.}}1+1=2. The error is ES=∫abf(x) dx−Sn.E_S = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx - S_n\mathclose{\text{.}}ES​=∫ab​f(x)dx−Sn​.

Simpson’s rule is in fact a weighted average of the other two. The points of S2nS_{2n}S2n​ are those of TnT_nTn​ together with the midpoints used by Mn,M_n\mathclose{\text{,}}Mn​, and grouping the terms shows that

S2n=Tn+2Mn3.S_{2n} = \frac{T_n + 2M_n}{3}.S2n​=3Tn​+2Mn​​.

Here, with T2=1724T_2 = \tfrac{17}{24}T2​=2417​ and M2=2435,M_2 = \tfrac{24}{35}\mathclose{\text{,}}M2​=3524​, 13(1724+4835)=17472520=S4.\tfrac13\big(\tfrac{17}{24} + \tfrac{48}{35}\big) = \tfrac{1747}{2520} = S_4\mathclose{\text{.}}31​(2417​+3548​)=25201747​=S4​. Since ET≈−2EM,E_T \approx -2E_M\mathclose{\text{,}}ET​≈−2EM​, the weights 1 and 2 make the two errors nearly cancel.

A rule built to be exact for parabolas turns out to be exact for more.

Theorem 11.9Simpson’s rule is exact for cubics

If fff is a polynomial of degree at most 3, then Sn=∫abf(x) dxS_n = \int_a^b f(x)\,dxSn​=∫ab​f(x)dx for every even n.n\mathclose{\text{.}}n.

Proof

SnS_nSn​ adds up the rule over pairs of subintervals, and the integral adds up over them too, so it is enough to show that the rule is exact on one pair, [m−h,m+h].[m - h, m + h]\mathclose{\text{.}}[m−h,m+h]. Substituting x=m+sx = m + sx=m+s and expanding the powers (m+s)k(m + s)^k(m+s)k writes fff as c0+c1(x−m)+c2(x−m)2+c3(x−m)3,c_0 + c_1(x - m) + c_2(x - m)^2 + c_3(x - m)^3\mathclose{\text{,}}c0​+c1​(x−m)+c2​(x−m)2+c3​(x−m)3, with constants cj.c_j\mathclose{\text{.}}cj​. The part c0+c1(x−m)+c2(x−m)2c_0 + c_1(x - m) + c_2(x - m)^2c0​+c1​(x−m)+c2​(x−m)2 is a parabola or a line, so the rule gives its integral exactly, by construction. For (x−m)3,(x - m)^3\mathclose{\text{,}}(x−m)3, the integral over [m−h,m+h][m - h, m + h][m−h,m+h] is 0, because the function is odd about m;m\mathclose{\text{;}}m; and the rule gives h3((−h)3+4⋅0+h3)=0\tfrac{h}{3}\big((-h)^3 + 4\cdot 0 + h^3\big) = 03h​((−h)3+4⋅0+h3)=0 too. Both the integral and the rule are linear (the value for a sum of functions is the sum of the values, and constant factors come out), so the rule is exact for f.f\mathclose{\text{.}}f.

∎

The error bound for Simpson’s rule involves the fourth derivative f(4).f^{(4)}\mathclose{\text{.}}f(4).

Theorem 11.10Error bound for Simpson’s rule

Let f(4)f^{(4)}f(4) be continuous on [a,b],[a, b]\mathclose{\text{,}}[a,b], and let KKK be a number with ∣f(4)(x)∣≤K\abs{f^{(4)}(x)} \le K​f(4)(x)​≤K for every xxx in [a,b].[a, b]\mathclose{\text{.}}[a,b]. Then, for every even n,n\mathclose{\text{,}}n,

∣ES∣≤K(b−a)5180n4.\abs{E_S} \le \frac{K(b - a)^5}{180n^4}.∣ES​∣≤180n4K(b−a)5​.

The proof uses the idea of the Going deeper box with a longer calculation, and this series omits it. The bound agrees with Theorem 11.9: for a cubic, f(4)=0,f^{(4)} = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}f(4)=0, so K=0K = 0K=0 and the error is 0. It shrinks like 1n4:\tfrac{1}{n^4}\mathclose{\text{:}}n41​: doubling nnn divides it by 24=16,2^4 = 16\mathclose{\text{,}}24=16, and for a smooth fff the error itself usually falls by about the same factor, as the Compute it box below shows. For ln⁡2,\ln 2\mathclose{\text{,}}ln2, f(4)(x)=24x5≤24f^{(4)}(x) = \tfrac{24}{x^5} \le 24f(4)(x)=x524​≤24 on [1,2],[1, 2]\mathclose{\text{,}}[1,2], and 24180n4≤10−6\tfrac{24}{180n^4} \le 10^{-6}180n424​≤10−6 needs n4≥133,334,n^4 \ge 133{,}334\mathclose{\text{,}}n4≥133,334, that is, n≥19.11.n \ge 19.11\mathclose{\text{.}}n≥19.11. With nnn even, n=20n = 20n=20 suffices: twenty subintervals, where the trapezoidal rule needed 409.

Compute itThe three rules side by side

Each rule is a few lines of Python. The test integral ∫01e−x2 dx\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx∫01​e−x2dx has no elementary antiderivative, but Python’s math.erf gives its value, π2erf⁡1,\tfrac{\sqrt\pi}{2}\operatorname{erf} 1\mathclose{\text{,}}2π​​erf1, to about 16 significant digits:

Python
import math

def midpoint(f, a, b, n):
    dx = (b - a)/n
    return dx*sum(f(a + (i + 0.5)*dx) for i in range(n))

def trapezoid(f, a, b, n):
    dx = (b - a)/n
    return dx*(f(a)/2 + sum(f(a + i*dx) for i in range(1, n)) + f(b)/2)

def simpson(f, a, b, n):                    # n must be even
    dx = (b - a)/n
    inner = sum((4 if i % 2 else 2)*f(a + i*dx) for i in range(1, n))
    return dx/3*(f(a) + inner + f(b))

Now the errors as nnn doubles, and the ratio of each error to the next:

Python
f = lambda x: math.exp(-x**2)
exact = math.sqrt(math.pi)/2*math.erf(1)        # the integral from 0 to 1
ns = [4, 8, 16, 32, 64]
rules = {'M': midpoint, 'T': trapezoid, 'S': simpson}
err = {r: [exact - rule(f, 0, 1, n) for n in ns] for r, rule in rules.items()}
print('  n        E_M        E_T        E_S')
for k, n in enumerate(ns):
    print(f'{n:3d}' + ''.join(f'{err[r][k]:11.2e}' for r in rules))
for r in rules:
    print(r, [round(err[r][k - 1]/err[r][k], 2) for k in range(1, len(ns))])
Output
  n        E_M        E_T        E_S
  4  -1.92e-03   3.84e-03  -3.12e-05
  8  -4.79e-04   9.59e-04  -1.99e-06
 16  -1.20e-04   2.40e-04  -1.25e-07
 32  -2.99e-05   5.99e-05  -7.79e-09
 64  -7.48e-06   1.50e-05  -4.87e-10
M [4.01, 4.0, 4.0, 4.0]
T [4.01, 4.0, 4.0, 4.0]
S [15.72, 15.95, 15.99, 16.0]

The midpoint and trapezoidal errors fall by a factor of 4 at each doubling, and Simpson’s by a factor close to 16, as their bounds in Theorems 11.8 and 11.10 do. With 16 subintervals Simpson’s rule is already within 2×10−72 \times 10^{-7}2×10−7 of the integral, closer than the trapezoidal rule with 64. The midpoint rule overestimates here, because the graph of e−x2e^{-x^2}e−x2 is concave down on (−12,12),\big(-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big)\mathclose{\text{,}}(−2​1​,2​1​), an interval that covers most of [0,1][0, 1][0,1] (more precisely, because f′(1)−f′(0)=−2ef'(1) - f'(0) = -\tfrac{2}{e}f′(1)−f′(0)=−e2​ is negative, in the estimate of the Going deeper box); and ET≈−2EME_T \approx -2E_MET​≈−2EM​ once more.

And choose x\sqrt xx​ on [0,1][0, 1][0,1] with Simpson’s rule, and double nnn again: the ratios are only about 2.8, because the derivatives of x\sqrt xx​ are unbounded near 0, and Theorem 11.10 does not apply.

Which rule to use

  • A smooth function given by a formula. Simpson’s rule, or a library routine. Doubling nnn is a practical check: for Simpson’s rule the error of S2nS_{2n}S2n​ is about 115(S2n−Sn),\tfrac{1}{15}(S_{2n} - S_n)\mathclose{\text{,}}151​(S2n​−Sn​), since S2n−Sn=ES(n)−ES(2n)≈16ES(2n)−ES(2n).S_{2n} - S_n = E_S(n) - E_S(2n) \approx 16E_S(2n) - E_S(2n)\mathclose{\text{.}}S2n​−Sn​=ES​(n)−ES​(2n)≈16ES​(2n)−ES​(2n). Library routines go further: they use adaptive rules, which keep halving the subintervals only where the integrand changes fast. The widget computes its accurate value of the integral that way, with Simpson’s rule.
  • Measurements. Readings at equally spaced times suit the trapezoidal rule, or Simpson’s rule when the number of intervals is even; the midpoint rule needs values at the midpoints, which you usually do not have. Readings at unequal spacing are added up as trapezoids, one interval at a time.
  • A kink or an infinite slope. The error bounds need a bounded f′′f''f′′ or f(4).f^{(4)}\mathclose{\text{.}}f(4). For x\sqrt xx​ on [0,1],[0, 1]\mathclose{\text{,}}[0,1], (x)′′=−14x−3/2\big(\sqrt x\big)'' = -\tfrac14x^{-3/2}(x​)′′=−41​x−3/2 is unbounded near 0, and doubling nnn divides the error of Simpson’s rule by only about 2.8, not 16. Split the interval at a kink, or remove the trouble with a substitution: x=t2x = t^2x=t2 turns ∫01x dx\int_0^1 \sqrt x\,dx∫01​x​dx into ∫012t2 dt,\int_0^1 2t^2\,dt\mathclose{\text{,}}∫01​2t2dt, which Simpson’s rule integrates exactly.
  • Very many subintervals. Every value of fff carries a rounding error of about 10−1610^{-16}10−16 of its size (Module 2), and adding up millions of them can add those errors up. A good rule with a moderate nnn is both faster and more accurate.
Watch out

Three slips with Simpson’s rule. (1) It needs an even number of subintervals: five readings give four intervals and can be used, six readings give five intervals and cannot (use the trapezoidal rule, or Simpson’s rule on four of the intervals and a trapezoid for the last). (2) The weights are 1,4,2,4,…,2,4,1,1, 4, 2, 4, \dots, 2, 4, 1\mathclose{\text{,}}1,4,2,4,…,2,4,1, starting and ending with 1 and with 4 next to each end. (3) The factor in front is Δx3,\tfrac{\Delta x}{3}\mathclose{\text{,}}3Δx​, not Δx2\tfrac{\Delta x}{2}2Δx​ as in the trapezoidal rule.
