What you learned

  • Integration by parts reverses the product rule: ∫u dv=uv−∫v du,\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du\mathclose{\text{,}}∫udv=uv−∫vdu, and ∫abfg′ dx=[fg]ab−∫abf′g dx\int_a^b f g'\,dx = \big[fg\big]_a^b - \int_a^b f'g\,dx∫ab​fg′dx=[fg]ab​−∫ab​f′gdx for definite integrals. Choose uuu to get simpler when differentiated (LIATE is a rough guide) and dvdvdv to be integrable. Repeat it, organise the rounds in a table, solve for an integral that comes back (∫exsin⁡x dx),\int e^x\sin x\,dx\mathclose{\text{),}}∫exsinxdx), or derive a reduction formula (∫sin⁡nx dx).\int \sin^n x\,dx\mathclose{\text{).}}∫sinnxdx).
  • Trigonometric integrals: for sin⁡mxcos⁡nx,\sin^m x\cos^n x\mathclose{\text{,}}sinmxcosnx, save one factor of an odd power and substitute, or use the half-angle identities sin⁡2x=12(1−cos⁡2x)\sin^2 x = \tfrac12(1 - \cos 2x)sin2x=21​(1−cos2x) and cos⁡2x=12(1+cos⁡2x);\cos^2 x = \tfrac12(1 + \cos 2x)\mathclose{\text{;}}cos2x=21​(1+cos2x); for tan⁡mxsec⁡nx,\tan^m x\sec^n x\mathclose{\text{,}}tanmxsecnx, save sec⁡2x\sec^2 xsec2x or sec⁡xtan⁡x.\sec x\tan x\mathclose{\text{.}}secxtanx. ∫sec⁡x dx=ln⁡∣sec⁡x+tan⁡x∣+C.\int \sec x\,dx = \ln\abs{\sec x + \tan x} + C\mathclose{\text{.}}∫secxdx=ln∣secx+tanx∣+C.
  • Trigonometric substitution: x=asin⁡θ,x = a\sin\theta\mathclose{\text{,}}x=asinθ, atan⁡θa\tan\thetaatanθ or asec⁡θa\sec\thetaasecθ removes a2−x2,\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}\mathclose{\text{,}}a2−x2​, a2+x2\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}a2+x2​ or x2−a2;\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}\mathclose{\text{;}}x2−a2​; on the ranges of θ\thetaθ in the table the square roots need no absolute value signs (the secant row is for x≥a),x \ge a\mathclose{\text{),}}x≥a), and a right triangle takes the answer back to x.x\mathclose{\text{.}}x. It gives the areas πr2\pi r^2πr2 of a disc and πab\pi abπab of an ellipse.
  • Partial fractions: divide first if the rational function is improper; then write it as a sum of terms A(x−r)j\dfrac{A}{(x - r)^j}(x−r)jA​ and Bx+C(x2+px+q)j.\dfrac{Bx + C}{(x^2 + px + q)^j}\mathclose{\text{.}}(x2+px+q)jBx+C​. The cover-up method finds the coefficients of distinct linear factors, because multiplying by x−rx - rx−r and letting x→rx \to rx→r isolates them.
  • Strategy: simplify, substitute, classify (parts, trigonometric, substitution, partial fractions, roots), try again. Check every antiderivative by differentiating it.
  • By computer: SymPy’s antiderivatives may differ from yours by a constant, drop absolute values or use complex logarithms; differentiate to check. Elementary functions need not have elementary antiderivatives: by Liouville’s theorem (quoted here, not proved) e−x2,e^{-x^2}\mathclose{\text{,}}e−x2, sin⁡xx\tfrac{\sin x}{x}xsinx​ and 1ln⁡x\tfrac{1}{\ln x}lnx1​ have none, and their antiderivatives are named by integrals: erf⁡,\operatorname{erf}\mathclose{\text{,}}erf, Si⁡,\operatorname{Si}\mathclose{\text{,}}Si, Li⁡.\operatorname{Li}\mathclose{\text{.}}Li.
  • Numerical integration: the midpoint rule Mn,M_n\mathclose{\text{,}}Mn​, the trapezoidal rule Tn=12(Ln+Rn)T_n = \tfrac12(L_n + R_n)Tn​=21​(Ln​+Rn​) and Simpson’s rule SnS_nSn​ (nnn even, weights 1,4,2,…,4,1).1, 4, 2, \dots, 4, 1\mathclose{\text{).}}1,4,2,…,4,1). With ∣f′′∣≤K,\abs{f''} \le K\mathclose{\text{,}}∣f′′∣≤K, ∣ET∣≤K(b−a)312n2\abs{E_T} \le \tfrac{K(b - a)^3}{12n^2}∣ET​∣≤12n2K(b−a)3​ and ∣EM∣≤K(b−a)324n2;\abs{E_M} \le \tfrac{K(b - a)^3}{24n^2}\mathclose{\text{;}}∣EM​∣≤24n2K(b−a)3​; with ∣f(4)∣≤K,\abs{f^{(4)}} \le K\mathclose{\text{,}}​f(4)​≤K, ∣ES∣≤K(b−a)5180n4.\abs{E_S} \le \tfrac{K(b - a)^5}{180n^4}\mathclose{\text{.}}∣ES​∣≤180n4K(b−a)5​. Doubling nnn divides the errors by about 4, 4 and 16; Simpson’s rule is exact for cubics; concavity gives the signs of ETE_TET​ and EM.E_M\mathclose{\text{.}}EM​.

Exercise 11.3★Partial fractions
  • (a) Find ∫x+7x2−x−6 dx.\displaystyle\int \frac{x + 7}{x^2 - x - 6}\,dx\mathclose{\text{.}}∫x2−x−6x+7​dx.

(c) The numerator and the denominator have the same degree, 2, so the fraction is improper, and Theorem 11.7 does not apply to it. In Exercise 9.9, a program logged a GPU’s power draw every 10 seconds during a one-minute job. The made-up readings were 120, 180, 250, 260, 240, 200 and 150 W at t=0,10,…,60t = 0, 10, \dots, 60t=0,10,…,60 s.

  • (b) Compare the trapezoidal estimate with the left and right sums of Exercise 9.9, 12,500 J and 12,800 J.

(a) There are n=6n = 6n=6 intervals of Δt=10\Delta t = 10Δt=10 s, an even number, so both rules apply:

T6=102[120+2(180+250+260+240+200)+150]=5⋅2530=12,650 J,S6=103[120+4⋅180+2⋅250+4⋅260+2⋅240+4⋅200+150]=103⋅3810=12,700 J.\begin{aligned} T_6 &= \frac{10}{2}\big[120 + 2(180 \\ &\qquad + 250 + 260 + 240 \\ &\qquad + 200) + 150\big] \\ &= 5\cdot 2530 = 12{,}650 \text{ J}, \\ S_6 &= \frac{10}{3}\big[120 + 4\cdot 180 \\ &\qquad + 2\cdot 250 + 4\cdot 260 \\ &\qquad + 2\cdot 240 + 4\cdot 200 \\ &\qquad + 150\big] \\ &= \frac{10}{3}\cdot 3810 \\ &= 12{,}700 \text{ J}. \end{aligned}T6​S6​​=210​[120+2(180+250+260+240+200)+150]=5⋅2530=12,650 J,=310​[120+4⋅180+2⋅250+4⋅260+2⋅240+4⋅200+150]=310​⋅3810=12,700 J.​

(b) T6=12,650T_6 = 12{,}650T6​=12,650 J is the average of 12,500 J and 12,800 J, as Definition 11.4 says it must be.

(c) M6M_6M6​ needs the power at the midpoints 5, 15, …, 55 s, which were not measured. With 3 subintervals of 20 s, though, the midpoints are 10, 30 and 50 s, which were: M3=20(180+260+200)=12,800M_3 = 20(180 + 260 + 200) = 12{,}800M3​=20(180+260+200)=12,800 J. With T3=202(120+2⋅250+2⋅240+150)=12,500T_3 = \tfrac{20}{2}(120 + 2\cdot 250 + 2\cdot 240 + 150) = 12{,}500T3​=220​(120+2⋅250+2⋅240+150)=12,500 J, the relation of Example 11.21 gives back Simpson’s estimate: 13(T3+2M3)=13(12,500+25,600)=12,700\tfrac13(T_3 + 2M_3) = \tfrac13(12{,}500 + 25{,}600) = 12{,}70031​(T3​+2M3​)=31​(12,500+25,600)=12,700 J =S6.= S_6\mathclose{\text{.}}=S6​. None of these estimates comes with a guarantee: ten-second readings say nothing about the power between them.
